news.title: Kamala Harris to Stump in Michigan with Socialist Abdul El-Sayed
news.text:
Failed Democrat presidential candidate Kamala Harris plans to campaign with Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed next week, their first joint public appearance since she endorsed the progressive Democrat.

The former vice president heads to Michigan to campaign for El-Sayed as national Democrats work to unite behind him. His primary win had exposed deep rifts within the party. Harris and El-Sayed have talked multiple times since she endorsed him after his August primary victory, though Tuesday marks their first joint public appearance, according to the Associated Press.

Harris and El-Sayed will attend a Tuesday roundtable focused on black maternal health, according to his campaign spokesperson. El-Sayed is a physician who once ran the health departments in Detroit and Wayne County.

Harris spokesperson Eduardo Negrón framed the visit as a turnout play in a state Democrats cannot afford to lose.

“Vice President Harris looks forward to returning to Michigan to help turn out the vote in this critical state,” Negrón said in a statement. “It is critical we flip the Senate so we can bring down prices and stand up to Donald Trump’s corruption.”

El-Sayed, whose full name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, faces Republican Mike Rogers in November. Rogers, a former U.S. representative, has repeatedly cast the Democrat as too extreme for the state.

“They believe that they can move the state and the country, by the way, to be more accepting of this socialism,” Rogers told Breitbart News, describing El-Sayed as the “Democratic Socialists of America darling right now” and calling the race “crazy versus common sense.”

Recent polling suggests a tight contest. A survey conducted for the Detroit News and WDIV-TV showed Rogers at 45.8 percent to El-Sayed’s 44.4 percent, reversing earlier surveys that had put the Democrat ahead.

When Harris endorsed El-Sayed in August, she praised his agenda while attacking Republicans.

“Dr. Abdul El-Sayed understands that the power is with the people, and that the stakes couldn’t be higher in this election,” Harris said at the time.

White House communications director Steven Cheung dismissed the endorsement, writing that Harris “should really re-evaluate her life choices before running for president again.”

Harris is stepping in as Democrats fight to keep the seat being vacated by retiring Sen. Gary Peters, one of several races that could tip control of the Senate. El-Sayed’s primary victory over Rep. Haley Stevens split the party, largely over U.S. support for Israel.
news.summary:
Failed Democrat presidential candidate Kamala Harris plans to campaign with Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed next week, their first joint public appearance since she endorsed the progressive Democrat.

news.title: Frail Mitch McConnell appears to need assist from fellow Republicans after he nearly votes wrong way in Senate
news.text:
Sen. Mitch McConnell appeared frail and required assistance from a fellow Republican senator at a committee hearing on Wednesday, two days after returning to the Hill for the first time since his hospitalization in June.

The Kentucky senator was at a meeting of the Senate Committee on Agriculture when his name was repeatedly called by a clerk recording the votes. Sen. John Boozman, a Republican from Arkansas, leaned in and instructed him to say “aye”.

McConnell then raised a finger and said, “aye,” and the votes continued.

The moment was quickly picked up online by Democrats who said that the senator had almost mistakenly voted with the wrong side.

“Republicans have to instruct Mitch McConnell to vote "yes" on a bill after he nearly votes "no" with Democrats,” wrote one account affiliated with the Democratic National Committee (DNC) and former vice president Kamala Harris.

Leaving the committee meeting afterwards, McConnell ignored questions from reporters outside as he was quickly wheeled away by aides.

The moment comes just two days after the senior Kentucky senator and former leader of the Republican conference returned from a months-long absence. He was hospitalized in June after a fall, and then developed pneumonia, according to statements released from his office. His return to Washington followed weeks in a rehabilitation center.

He smiled and gave a thumbs-up to reporters as he was wheeled by aides out of his D.C. home on his way to the Senate on Monday, but did not take questions from reporters or respond to shouted inquiries. Spectators and online viewers noted that he seemed to stare straight ahead, his mouth partially agape.

He hasn’t given an on-camera statement at length since his hospitalization. Before returning to Washington, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear repeatedly urged his office to release a video of the senator talking about his recovery, but was rebuffed.

The Independent reached out to the senator’s office for comment.

At 84, McConnell is in his last term in the Senate. He announced last year that he would not stand for re-election, shortly after stepping down as leader of the Republican Senate conference and allowing his close ally Sen. John Thune to take over.

A former sufferer of childhood polio, McConnell has suffered repeated falls before, including on Capitol Hill, and over the past year has typically used a wheelchair to get around the Hill with the assistance of aides. One of the falls he suffered in 2023 occurred in public at Washington’s Reagan airport and was described as a “face-plant”.

Age has become a serious point of contention in Washington and particularly on Capitol Hill, where aging lawmakers in both chambers have faced accusations of remaining in office long after they are unable to effectively serve. Instances of such lawmakers suffering from bouts of confusion or disorientation have been reported involving members of both parties.

McConnell is no stranger to these concerns himself and alarmed many in the media and in the Senate itself when, in two moments within a few days of each other in the summer of 2023, he appeared to freeze up and be unable to speak at two news conferences on the Hill, surrounded by his colleagues and journalists.

On Monday, he described his recovery process after his latest hospitalization as sometimes frustrating, but said he was glad to be back in Washington.

“Today, I’ll cast my first Senate vote since I took a bad fall back in June. I’m really looking forward to being back on the Senate floor and seeing my colleagues,” said McConnell in a statement released to news outlets.

“My recovery has been a long and often frustrating process, and the lingering effects of childhood polio haven’t made it any easier. I’m still not quite back to 100%, but I’ve assured Leader Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me,” his statement continued. “Elaine and I are very grateful for all the continued well wishes from our fellow Kentuckians, and I’m glad to get back to more of business as usual on their behalf this month.”
news.summary: McConnell is accused of nearly voting with Democrats by mistake at Agriculture committee meeting
news.author: John Bowden

news.title: Republicans Get Warning Sign as Four 'Safe' Seats Shift Toward Democrats
news.text: Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifted eight races toward Democrats, including four previously thought to be safe GOP seats, on Wednesday—the latest warning sign for Republicans ahead of the November midterms. The changes come as Democrats are hoping to expand the battleground to compete in more conservative areas in this year’s elections. President Donald Trump’s approval rating has slipped to record lows in the latest polls amid growing frustration over the economy and cost of living. Democrats believe that could give them opportunities to flip more seats in Congress this year, even in states and districts that backed Trump by large margins in 2024. Democrats have also expanded their polling lead in the past few weeks. Democrats held an 8.6-point lead in RealClearPolitics’ aggregate of generic ballot polls. That’s the largest lead they’ve had so far this cycle and represents nearly a two-point leftward shift from one month earlier, when their lead stood at 6.8 points. That average is also identical to Democrats’ popular vote victory in 2018, when they rode a “blue wave” to flip more than 40 seats in the House of Representatives. Which Seats Changed in Sabato’s Crystal Ball New Ratings? The following seats shifted in the latest ratings from Sabato’s Crystal Ball: These sorts of seats could present Democrats with chances to cut into the GOP majority to establish a greater majority in a “blue wave” national environment. Many of these districts voted for Trump by double digits or have a history of voting. If Democrats make these races competitive, it would be a sign of a stronger blue wave. Currently, Republicans hold a slim majority with 218 seats compared to Democrats’ 214 seats and one independent, so Democrats only have to flip a handful of seats to win a majority. But winning tougher races would be beneficial, giving them more room for defections on key legislative priorities. Kyle Kondik, managing editor of Sabato’s Crystal Ball, wrote in the update that Republicans are facing an “enthusiasm problem” ahead of November, and that an effort to motivate the base by holding a convention in Texas “does not as of yet appear to be paying dividends.” “Those waiting for a Republican recovery in the polls will have to keep waiting, and the wait may be for Godot,” he wrote. “The post-Labor Day period has seen the Democrats generally doing well in surveys. The most-watched one was the New York Times/Siena University House generic ballot poll released Tuesday morning: Democrats were up 8.5 points.” Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee Communications Director Courtney Rice told Newsweek that Americans are “sick of rising prices and broken promises, and they’re ready to elect Democrats to the House Majority in November.” “While House Republicans are stuck trying to defend rising gas prices and the war in Iran, Democrats are on offense and poised to win in districts that voted for Trump by double digits,” Rice said. Newsweek also reached out to the National Republican Congressional Committee for comment via email. Democrats Gain in Safe Republican Seats Four of the shifts came in seats previously not viewed as competitive. Republicans are still favored in these races, but they are now viewed as being more engaged by the elections forecaster. “Things may end up bad enough for Republicans that we might see upsets in some places we don’t expect,” Kondik wrote. Here is a look at where things stand in each of these races. Arkansas’ 2nd District Republican Representative French Hill is facing a challenge from Democrat Chris Jones, an engineer and former gubernatorial candidate, in a Republican-leaning district. The district is based around Little Rock, a Democratic city, but also includes more conservative, rural areas across the central region of Arkansas. It backed Trump by nearly 16 points in 2024. Jones has received the endorsement of former Vice President Kamala Harris, but it’s not clear that national Democrats are prepared to invest in this seat. However, Republicans have begun putting money into this seat. “Hill recently benefited from about $400,000 in outside spending from a new Republican Super PAC, a development reported by Politico that raised our eyebrows a bit in a Trump +15ish district,” Kondik wrote. Nevada’s 2nd District This Nevada district has started to garner some attention, despite the fact that it backed Trump by 14 points in 2024. The vast district includes large swaths of rural areas in the northern part of the state, but many voters live in the Reno and Carson City areas. Historically, it has a Republican lean and has been represented by Republican Representative Mark Amodei since 2011. Amodei, who has overperformed other Republicans in the district, is retiring at the end of the term. His retirement leaves the seat open and has driven up Democrats’ hopes that they could pull off a surprise victory. A recent poll showed a closer race than expected, but still found a large number of voters are undecided. The GBAO poll, sponsored by a Democratic group, Nevada Alliance, found Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson, the former leader of the Nevada Assembly, with a single-point lead over former Air Force Lieutenant Colonel David Flippo, 38 to 37 percent. Independent American Party candidate Lynn Chapman also received 14 percent in the poll. It surveyed 500 likely voters from August 31 to September 3 and was first reported by The Nevada Independent. New York’s 21st District Republican Representative Elise Stefanik has won by large margins in this district, based around North Country. Once a more competitive area, the region has swung rightward over the past decade, backing Trump by more than 20 points in the last election. But Stefanik’s retirement has brought new attention to the seat. Businessman Anthony Constantino, a Republican, and Democrat Blake Gendebien, a dairy farmer, are running to succeed her in the House. A new poll of the district gave Constantino a modest lead. The Public Policy Polling/The Bench survey showed him up 5 points, 48 percent to 43 percent. It surveyed 557 registered voters from September 9 to 10, 2026, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.2 percentage points. Blake Gendebien has received support from the Blue Dog PAC, a coalition supporting moderate Democrats. He told Newsweek in February 2025, when he was running for a special election that was canceled after Trump pulled Stefanik’s nomination to become United Nations ambassador, that Trump’s tariffs could make the district, which has close ties to Canada, more competitive. "We buy 80 percent of our potash fertilizer from Canada. This will impact the North Country and the entire United States. Corn, soybeans, and also forage, alfalfa, we require it. We need that fertilizer," he said at the time. "If there's a 25 percent tariff on that, all of our food is going to get more expensive. There's no way around it." Ohio’s 10th District This district is, in theory, more competitive than the other districts. It voted for Trump by fewer than 8 points in 2024, and it’s based around Dayton, which has many Democratic voters. “But he has been an excellent performer even in tough years, so he’s not as vulnerable as the partisan topline might suggest,” Kondik wrote. Republican Representative Michael Turner is a strong incumbent who has won by large margins in the past despite the district being only light red. He is facing a challenge from Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker, a veteran. Turner has drawn credible challenges in the past but has been able to withstand stronger Democratic environments. Other Rating Changes The other changes are in races that were already thought to be competitive. Democrats’ Chances of Taking Back House: Polls Democrats have led generic ballot polls throughout 2026, but some surveys showed a tighter margin that would suggest a blue ripple, rather than a wave. But that’s changing, with recent surveys giving Democrats an expanded lead, some showing a double-digit advantage. The latest poll from YouGov and The Economist gave Democrats a 12-point lead among 1,051 likely voters, 51 percent to 39 percent. Six percent were still undecided, and 3 percent said they would vote for another party. The poll highlights the GOP’s motivation problem. Among all registered voters, Democrats only led by 5 points, 44 percent to 39 percent. It was conducted from September 11 to 14, 2026. Democrats had a 7-point lead in the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll, 44 percent to 37 percent. It surveyed 896 registered voters from September 11 to 14, 2026. Meanwhile, The New York Times and Siena University released a poll giving Democrats a 9-point lead, 51 percent to 43 percent. It surveyed 1,503 likely voters from September 8 to 13, 2026. What Does Democrats’ Generic Ballot Lead Mean for the Midterms? It’s difficult to project exactly how a generic ballot lead would translate to the number of seat pickups for Democrats, especially as mid-decade redistricting has cast a level of uncertainty over the elections. But if that polling advantage holds up on Election Day, it could point to a more comfortable majority for Democrats. Here is a look at how recent elections have gone. What Happens Next Polls will continue to be closely watched ahead of November 3. Issues like the economy, cost of living, the Iran war, and AI could shape the contours of the midterms as candidates make their pitches to voters over the coming months. news.summary: Safe Republican seats shifted in Arkansas, Nevada, New York and Ohio, as Democrats expand their polling lead ahead of November.

news.title: Democrats embraced AI’s growth before Trump came along; now, they want to slow it down
news.text: Some of the Democratic Party’s most prominent voices are pushing for tighter limits on artificial intelligence, including former President Barack Obama, who has joined calls for a slower pace of frontier AI development after years of Democratic leaders touting the technology’s economic and strategic potential. "We need government — and specifically our leaders in Washington — to get proactive in coming up with concrete proposals, laws and regulations that deal with serious safety concerns, anticipate AI’s impact on jobs and our kids and make sure that AI’s benefits are widely spread," Obama said in a statement Monday night. Obama’s latest comments put greater emphasis on slowing frontier AI development than his White House did in 2016, when his administration highlighted the technology’s economic potential while also warning about disruption and calling for policy responses. AI EXTINCTION WARNINGS DOMINATE HEADLINES AFTER EX-ANTHROPIC EMPLOYEE'S VIRAL POST Democrats have long paired enthusiasm for AI’s economic and strategic potential with warnings about its risks, but some of the party’s most prominent voices are now going further, calling for a slower pace of frontier AI development and tougher limits on how the technology is built and deployed. Attorney General Todd Blanche argued Tuesday that Democrats’ renewed focus on the potential risks of artificial intelligence should not be treated as "breaking news," suggesting the timing, months before the midterm elections, is politically significant. "Every Democrat senator suddenly races to a microphone to talk about AI after being eerily silent for months and months, a month. So, to talk about the timing of this as being nothing but an effort to influence the midterms, I shouldn't have to say that out loud, of course," said Blanche. The comments came as President Donald Trump has made rapid AI development and the data centers needed to power it a priority, while the administration promotes the technology’s potential economic benefits and faces growing political scrutiny over the cost and impact of expanding data-center infrastructure. Obama issued a statement Monday on X, writing that AI is "moving at lightning speed – and even faster than those who are engineering it can keep up with." "Given what we know about technology, we can’t stuff AI back in a box. But we can collectively determine how it's developed and how it’s used, rather than sitting back and letting AI and its fallout happen to us," he wrote. He called for regulation, saying choices to slow down should not be left up to the tech companies. Any "potential catastrophe will depend on the choices that we make right now," said Obama. ANTHROPIC CEO CALLS ON AI INDUSTRY TO SLOW DOWN TECH RACE, DRAWING SUPPORT FROM ELON MUSK, SAM ALTMAN In 2016, Obama’s White House touted AI’s potential to open new markets and drive progress across industries while warning about job disruption and broader safety and policy challenges. "Advances in AI technology hold incredible potential to help the United States stay on the cutting edge of innovation," the White House said in its December 2016 Artificial Intelligence, Automation, and the Economy report. "Advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology and related fields have opened up new markets and new opportunities for progress in critical areas such as health, education, energy, economic inclusion, social welfare, and the environment. … AI should be welcomed for its potential economic benefits," the report added. Similarly, then-Vice President Kamala Harris said in January 2025 that "it is imperative that the United States remain the global leader on AI" as the Biden administration moved to speed up the buildout needed to support large-scale AI operations. The Biden administration announced an executive order aimed at accelerating AI infrastructure in the U.S., including large data centers and clean-energy projects, as the administration sought to keep the country ahead of its global competitors. Harris has also recently called for slowing the pace of frontier AI development, arguing that the technology is advancing at an "alarming speed" and urging Congress to establish stronger oversight and safety standards. "The frontier of artificial intelligence is advancing at an alarming speed. Over the weekend, industry leaders voiced support for an idea that the American people and many AI researchers in their own labs have been calling for: We must responsibly slow the pace of frontier AI development," she wrote. SEVEN-FIGURE BLITZ AS GOP EMBRACES PUSH TO COMPETE WITH CHINA IN BOOMING NEW TECH SPACE AI and data centers have quickly become a major midterm issue, as concerns over electricity costs, jobs and the rapid buildout draw increasing attention from candidates in both parties. news.summary: Barack Obama is urging Washington to slow AI development. But, in 2016, his White House praised the technology as the cutting edge of innovation.

news.title: Newsom’s support for 2028 presidential bid tanks, AOC and other contenders rise: poll
news.text:
Gov. Gavin Newsom is slipping in 2028 presidential polls, as other Democrats pick up steam.

A new Bowling Green State University/YouGov poll found Newsom had dipped to third-place pick for the Democratic nominee with 14% support. That’s behind former VP Kamala Harris (17%) and former Biden Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg (16%).

Newsom led the pack in a February YouGov poll and has typically been in the top 2 with Harris. He told CNN this week he won’t launch his White House bid if Harris, a fellow Californian, puts her hat in the ring for a third try at the presidency, citing “mutually assured destruction.”

The latest poll, conducted Aug. 25 through Sept. 1, shows Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) gaining momentum. 

The Squad rep is tied with Newsom in third place at 14%, followed by Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ) at 10%. 

AOC said in an August interview that she “hasn’t ruled out the possibility” of running in 2028, and that she’s focused on winning the 2026 midterms.

Buttigieg’s support has also grown this year, as Newsom falters. Kelly has also been making early presidential moves by visiting early voting states and raising his profile.

YouGov’s latest September poll was conducted with 1200 US registered voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.3 percentage points. It did not survey voters about Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA), who is polling favorably in other surveys. 

The Post reached out to Harris’s, Newsom’s, AOC’s, Buttigieg’s, and Kelly’s offices and did not receive an immediate response.
news.summary: Gov. Gavin Newsom is slipping in 2028 presidential polls, as other Democrats pick up steam.

news.title: Gavin Newsom Is Back on Top of One 2028 List. Does It Mean Anything?
news.text:
In veteran political reporter Mark Halperin's July rankings of potential 2028 Democratic presidential nominees, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) was rising, while Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-Calif.) was losing momentum. Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) candidates had just achieved huge victories in New York and Colorado primaries the previous month, and Halperin declared that the toughest thing to do in Democratic politics was to stop a socialist from becoming the presidential nominee.

Newsom slipped from first place to second place in August. Now, in Halperin's September rankings, he's back on top. What changed?

Halperin compiles his monthly rankings by asking more than 60 analysts, mostly Democrats, whom they think is most likely to become the party's 2028 nominee. Despite placing Newsom first in July, Halperin believed the governor would ultimately decide not to run because he is the subject of U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) investigations.

Sanders, who ranked third in July behind Newsom and Gov. Josh Shapiro (D-Pa.), was one of three candidates in Halperin's top eight that month from what he called the "Mamdani wing of the Democratic Party." Halperin was bullish on the Vermont senator because he believed the Democratic establishment was weaker than ever and that candidates from the establishment wing realized they had to "cater to the progressive wing."

That brings us back to Newsom. Halperin now thinks the governor has figured out how to do just that: appeal to the Democratic Party's socialist wing. He points to a Sept. 7 PBS interview Newsom gave in South Carolina in which he was asked where he stands on the DSA. Newsom answered: "If it's about more money in your pocket, lowering costs ... getting money out of politics and ... about Medicare for all, I think we're pretty aligned." While most Republicans can't listen to a word the hand-gesticulating governor says without thinking "phony," Halperin praised the answer's "sophistication":

I've not heard Chuck Schumer, Hakeem Jeffries, or any other potential presidentials talk about a big tent with such confidence and clarity as Newsom did in that one answer. And that's a testament not only to the prospect that he can win some of those votes, even if there's a socialist in the race if he runs, and that he can keep the party united the way Hillary Clinton struggled to do in 2016, part of why she didn't beat Donald Trump, but that he has a lot of savvy and a lot of confidence.And people underrate the ability that he has to think through and speak. It's kind of ironic because one of the biggest raps against him is he's inauthentic. A lot of people say that about him. That's not what I think about him.

What about another potential candidate whom so many find inauthentic: Kamala Harris? Newsom recently told Jake Tapper while the two were fly-fishing that he wouldn't run for president if the former vice president decided to run because it would be "mutual assured destruction." Halperin took that mysterious answer into consideration but ultimately kept Newsom at number one. Although Harris, like Newsom, would be able to raise a lot of money, he agrees with those who believe she won't run. For that reason, she lands at number six on his list.

Gov. Shapiro, who appears poised to cruise to reelection, is another candidate who can raise money. Halperin still has him in the number two position, but last I checked, he's still Jewish, so I think that's way too high for a party with an out-of-control antisemitism problem.

Being gay and short may be less of a problem than being Jewish. Halperin acknowledges that many people write off Pete Buttigieg, number three on the list, because of those two characteristics, but he thinks he's a strong contender for three reasons: He knows how to campaign, win votes, and build coalitions. The big question remains whether he can win over black voters, which he wasn't able to do the last time he ran.

These names make up the so-called "establishment" wing of the Democratic Party, although the establishment and socialist wings are becoming increasingly difficult to distinguish. As Victor Davis Hanson notes, "Democratic Socialists became mainstream largely by imitating an increasingly socialist Democratic Party."

 Related: Bernie Rising: Is Sanders Becoming a 2028 Frontrunner?

As for the more unabashedly socialist candidates, Halperin ranks Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y., 14th District) at number four, ahead of Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) at number seven, although he is not certain that she'll run — despite speculation concerning her decision to freeze her eggs.

And I continue to believe that one of the biggest moments that's coming in the presidential nomination fight for the Democrats is when AOC and Bernie sit down and have conversations, which I suspect they'll do right after the midterms. Which one of them's going to run? And if neither of them's going to run, the Democrats are going to face a problem. But I believe that if she does run, she will be the consensus socialist choice—progressive choice—even though a lot of progressives think, ironically, she's too moderate.

The takeaway from Halperin's admittedly way-too-early horse-race prognostication is that some of the leading contenders might not even enter the race.

One name we can rule out, however, is Zohran Mamdani. If the names on Halperin's list are too depressing for you to contemplate, at least take comfort in the fact that the New York City mayor isn't among them.

news.title: Trump accuses Democrats of mishandling his assassination attempt probe
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has claimed that an FBI probe into his attempted assassination in July 2024 was deliberately mishandled as part of a “Democrat plot” to prevent him from winning a second term. He also referred to “new info” that supposedly appeared in the case, but provided no details.

In 2024, Trump, then the Republican presidential candidate, narrowly escaped death at a campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, when a 20-year-old man fired shots from a rooftop, grazing Trump’s ear and killing one attendee and injuring two others.

Trump claimed at the time that President Joe Biden and his Democratic rival, Kamala Harris, were partly to blame as they allegedly made it more difficult for the Secret Service to protect him, while peddling rhetoric that could have encouraged the shooter.

The would-be assassin, Thomas M. Crooks, was killed by the US Secret Service. An internal review released later that year concluded that the Secret Service made multiple mistakes ahead of the shooting.

“Everybody knows the Crooked Joe Biden FBI didn’t do what they should have with respect to the Lunatic who shot me in Butler,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social on Tuesday.

He also claimed that “most of the information [on the case] was missing, altered, corrupted, or gone” by the time he took office in January 2025. “This was all a Democrat Plot, to get me out of the Election, that failed,” the president stated, adding that some new information on the case had emerged recently, but provided no details.

Trump also blamed former FBI Director Christopher Wray for mishandling the probe and maintained he “should pay a price for the way he handled this assassination attempt, and certainly for the things he said.”

Wray, who was nominated by Trump himself during his first term in office, stated that his agency did not find any accomplices of the shooter during testimony to the House Judiciary Committee. He also said it was unclear if Trump had been hit directly by a bullet or by shrapnel, provoking sharp criticism from Trump at the time. Wray resigned before Trump’s inauguration in January 2025.

The current FBI director, Kash Patel, told the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday that his agency looked into Crooks’ possible connection to any accomplices but found none. “We found no evidence that that individual was literally even speaking to any other human being other than his parents, who he resided with,” he said.

Attorney General Todd Blanche mentioned during the same hearing that new information related to the case had surfaced recently. “It is new information about the shooter and about his background, about his history and that’s stuff that we didn’t know before,” he said while refusing to elaborate.

Trump has been targeted in several assassination attempts. Two months after the July 2024 incident, a pro-Ukraine activist was arrested after being spotted with a rifle near Trump’s golf course in Florida. He was later found guilty of trying to assassinate Trump.

In April 2026, the president and First Lady Melania Trump were rushed from the Washington Hilton after gunfire broke out at the White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner. The suspect, Cole Tomas Allen, was later charged with attempting to assassinate the president as well.
news.summary:
US President Donald Trump has accused Democrats of mishandling the investigation into his attempted assassination in July 2024

news.title: How Kamala Harris’ campaign lied about Beyonce, Taylor Swift and Bad Bunny to attract and exploit crowds
news.text:
For years, Lindy Li was an extremely active member of the Democratic Party. A former financial analyst, she ran for Congress in 2018 but lost in the Democratic primary. She went on to become a key fundraiser for the DNC, raising millions for Joe Biden’s presidential campaign in 2020 and Kamala Harris’ in 2024. But, in the wake of Harris’ defeat, dismayed with what she’d seen and how money had been spent, she had a highly publicized break from the party, which she details in her new book, “Unburdened: A Former Democrat Insider’s Shocking Account of Political Power, Betrayal, and Party Collapse” (Harper, Sept. 22). “I don’t think I could have lived with myself had I not told the truth,” she recently told Fox News. In this excerpt, she writes of how the Harris campaign lied about celebrities such as Beyonce and Taylor Swift to attract and exploit crowds.

Beyoncé will perform on the final night of the convention!

Just kidding — that was just a lie to pack the stadium for Kamala’s acceptance speech.

Deceit slithered through Chicago like Dementors from “Harry Potter,” chilling the air as fifty thousand delegates, alternates, volunteers and press descended upon Carl Sandburg’s “Hog Butcher for the World.” 

As a member of the National Finance Committee, I was ushered in as a VIP, gliding from our hotel to the United Center in a private shuttle that looped through the city’s veins.

But the moment Beyoncé failed to take the convention stage, disillusionment spilled into plain view. True to form, Team B.O.C.H. — the name I’d given Biden, Obama, Clinton and Harris — botched the optics with spectacular ineptitude, courting worldwide ridicule and accusations of deceit. 

Older Americans may not comprehend the power this pop demigod wields over the liberal faithful, but by willfully fanning the flames of the wildfire rumors, they effectively swore to the surging throngs — chiefly younger voters, an indispensable electoral force — that Queen Bey would serenade the masses. When she didn’t, the betrayal clanged with cataclysmic force, raw, ruthless, and ragingly ruinous. Harris face-planted before the very voters she needed most.

The singer P!nk wasn’t a big enough artist to fill Beyoncé’s towering stilettos. Alex observed that historians would pinpoint the Beyoncé debacle as the tipping point, the moment the campaign’s sugar high crashed into a brutal hangover, highlighting Harris’s ineptitude at political pageantry and her inability to follow through on her massive promises. In politics, as in life, perception is reality; the court of public opinion either dooms or deifies.

The DNC’s boneheaded showmanship hit a new low in Houston at a high-profile rally on Oct. 25. Less than two weeks ahead of the election, they once again dangled Beyoncé like forbidden fruit, only to snatch it away a second time, igniting a righteous rage that rippled through the ranks. Queen Bey, loved for her anthems, not her analyses, gave a speech that no one wanted. She had performed for Clinton in 2016, only for Trump’s win to splatter egg on her sequins. Perhaps she was done wagering her crown on another politician. When Harris took the stage after Bey’s letdown, she was greeted by furious howls, serpents of humanity streaming toward the exits. Team Harris wielded celebrities as crowd-wrangling bait, a tacit admission

In the campaign’s ebbing final hours, a VIP summons thunked in my inbox: an invitation to Vice President Harris’s valedictory rally, promising a lineup of mystery superstars, right here in Philadelphia, the aorta of the swing states. For a full week, Kamala’s rumor factory cranked at full throttle, recycling the playbook they had used to generate hype for Beyoncé’s twice-teased, twice-thwarted appearances: first at the convention, then at the Houston rally. The stage was set for history. Or, as it turned out, for the most expensive karaoke night in American political memory.

To build mystique around their pièce de résistance, Kamala’s hype arsonists torched what little credibility they had left in one sun-kissed conflagration of rumor: Taylor Swift, Pennsylvania’s prodigal daughter, was allegedly descending from the pop-star heavens in a blaze of sequins and voter registration forms to electrify a race that had flatlined for weeks.

The night before the election, Fox News journalist Jacqui Heinrich suggested to me that it would be Taylor. Citing his own Vatican-level infallibility, a high-ranking Biden White House official said with absolute certainty that it was going to be Bad Bunny. Campaign czars swore it would be a chart-incinerating rock star, not a recently dumped has-been desperate to scrape together more sales on the worst-reviewed album of the year.

A fellow megabundler pinged his jealously guarded hunch: Beyoncé, stung by the backlash to her two non-performances and desiring redemption, would make the third time the charm.

Theories swirled like fanfic plot twists: Why Taylor? Home-state halo. Bey? Redemption arc. Bad Bunny? Youthquake bait. Pop’s pantheon had to descend — it simply had to. No universe existed where Kamala would shaft young Americans yet again, belly-flopping before the nation’s glare, with the entire globe thirsting like coyotes for the next overlong heehaw or word salad.

So, you can imagine the universal disappointment when the mystery guest was unmasked once more as Katy Perry, ready to bumble through the songs she wrote with an accused sex pest to a crowd of single-issue #MeToo voters. This was a con executed with sociopathic detachment. They dangled Taylor, Beyoncé, and Bad Bunny overhead like manna, luring thirty thousand shivering masochists onto frozen concrete, and the internet flambéed itself in a frenzy of speculation.

By the time Katy bounced out waving a sparkler nobody wanted, the footage was already cut, the headlines were locked, and the dopamine had been strip-mined. But instead of a single villain, there was a syndicate of deceit, each pocketing a succulent slice of the scam. Kamala, Queen Con, reaped rivers of rapturous ink and Instagram idolatry, snagging her Rocky moment. Her optics-obsessed staffers got their crowds. Media moguls milked the ad dollars. Influencers surfed the clickbait tsunami.

news.title: Ken Paxton Within Striking Distance of Defeating Talarico in New Texas Poll
news.text: Democratic Senate nominee in Texas James Talarico holds a narrow 3-point lead over Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton in a new poll released less than two months out from Election Day. The poll's margin of error is plus or minus 4 percentage points, so the narrow gap represents a dead heat in the key race that Democrats hope gets them over the hump in their long pursuit of capturing a statewide election in the firmly red state. The close gap comes as Paxton, the state's current attorney general, has seen Talarico gain momentum with leads in a number of polls as he has surged to become the favorite among prediction markets and political handicappers. Democrats have a narrow path to reclaim control of the upper chamber, where Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority, and stealing a longtime GOP seat from a state that backed President Donald Trump by more than 13 points in 2024 would be a huge gain. Democrats also must defend their current seats—including in two states Trump won in 2024—and flip four others. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party historically loses seats. Millions of dollars have already been spent on the Texas race, and both campaigns are ramping up outreach as they battle for undecided and independent voters in the final weeks of the campaign. "Democrats are running competitive Senate races in Ohio and Texas, a real indication that Republicans nationwide face significant headwinds. Being competitive and winning, though, are different concepts," Matt Klink, owner and president of Klink Campaigns, told Newsweek in a Wednesday email. Newsweek has reached out to Paxton and Talarico for comment via email on Wednesday. Texas Senate Race Texas last elected a Democrat to the Senate in 1988 and has backed Republican presidential nominees in every election since 1980, but Democrats think 2026 offers one of their best opportunities in years to compete statewide. Trump carried Texas by 13.7 percentage points in 2024, defeating then-Vice President Kamala Harris 56 percent to around 42.5 percent. The state has not elected a Democrat to statewide office since 1994, making it one of the nation's longest-running Republican strongholds. Democrats have repeatedly targeted the state as demographic shifts and population growth have reshaped the electorate, but they have fallen short in a series of closely watched campaigns, including Beto O'Rourke's narrow 2018 Senate loss to Ted Cruz. Describing the Senate race and Texas' political landscape, Klink added, "Talarico has real appeal to the national media and some Texas Democrats, but no Democrat has won a Texas Senate race since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988. Bentsen wouldn't even be considered a Democrat today." Polls show Paxton, who is endorsed by Trump, and Talarico, who has served as a state representative since 2018, holding narrow leads at different points in the campaign. The matchup follows Paxton's defeat of longtime Senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary in late May. Republicans descended on Dallas last week for the party’s unprecedented midterm convention. The convention is part of a plan to mobilize the GOP base ahead of November. Forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball consider the Texas race to be a toss-up. Ken Paxton vs James Talarico: What the Polls Show The new Mason-Dixon Polling & Research Inc. survey of 625 registered Texas voters found Talarico leading 46 percent to Paxton’s 43 percent. About 8 percent of participants were undecided and 3 percent backed libertarian candidate Ted Brown. The survey showed a gender divide, with Talarico leading women voters’ 52 percent to 36 percent and Paxton leading men 51 percent to 39 percent. Voter preferences are divided across age groups, with each candidate holding advantages among different generations. Talarico led voters ages 18 to 34 by a 51 percent to 37 percent margin and voters ages 50 to 64 by 49 percent to 41 percent, while Paxton led voters ages 35 to 49, 47 percent to 42 percent, and voters 65 and older, 46 percent to 45 percent. Regional support varied significantly across the state. Paxton's strongest support was concentrated in East Texas, where he led 58 percent to 38 percent, while Talarico ran strongest in Central Texas, posting a 57 percent to 31 percent advantage. Other polls also show a tight race. A new SoCal Strategies poll shows Talarico ahead with 50 percent of the vote compared to Paxton's 45 percent. The figures mark a shift from the pollster's June survey, which had Paxton leading 49 percent to 47 percent. The survey was conducted between September 12 and September 13 among 649 likely voters. That poll shows Talarico polling better than Beto O'Rourke was at this point in the 2018 campaign, when he went up against Senator Ted Cruz. At this point in the 2018 campaign, Cruz was leading O'Rourke by about 3 points, according to a Real Clear Politics average of polls. Cruz would go on to beat O'Rourke by about 2.6 percentage points in the election. A recent YouGov/Univision poll of 1,000 registered voters conducted between August 27 and September 4 found Talarico leading by 5 points, 48 percent to 43 percent. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points. An Overton Insights/Texas Public Policy Foundation poll of 1,167 likely voters from August 24-26 found Talarico and Paxton locked in a statistical dead heat. The poll found Talarico leading with 44 percent support to Paxton's 43.4 percent, while 12.6 percent of respondents remained undecided. When leaners were included, the race was effectively tied, with both candidates receiving 50 percent support. While the race remains highly competitive, prediction markets have recently tilted toward Talarico. On Wednesday, Kalshi gave the Democrat a 54 percent chance of winning, while Polymarket placed his odds at 56 percent. Scrutiny Surrounding The Candidates Republicans have cast Talarico as a progressive out of step with Texas voters, pointing to his policy positions, lifestyle, and comments on Christianity, while Democrats have focused on Paxton’s legal and political controversies, arguing he is unethical and corrupt. Paxton’s past, including criminal charges and allegations of infidelity, has been brought up on the national stage, both by the Democrats and earlier this year by his primary challenger, Cornyn. He was impeached by the Republican-controlled Texas House in 2023 on 20 articles against him, including allegations of abuse of office and bribery, though he was later acquitted by the Texas Senate. Paxton has maintained that the proceedings were politically motivated and has denied wrongdoing. In 2020, a group of people who worked with Paxton reported him to the FBI, alleging that he was abusing his office to prop up Paul, a political donor and real estate investor. Some of the workers resigned, and others were fired, leading to a suit under the Texas Whistleblower Act. Years later, in 2025, a Travis County district court judge concluded the aides were improperly fired and awarded them $6.6 million. Paxton initially filed an appeal but then dropped it after announcing his Senate campaign. In 2015, Paxton was indicted on felony securities fraud charges, which, had he been convicted, would have carried decades in prison. Earlier, he was accused of misleading investors. John Feehery, a partner at EFB Advocacy who previously served in the House Republican leadership, told Newsweek in an email, "Paxton is well-known figure in Texas, having won statewide several times. Love him or hate him, he has shown an ability to close and win." Dave Hopkins, a political science professor at Boston College, previously told Newsweek, "Ken Paxton’s scandal-ridden past seems to be a serious liability." Talarico has faced criticism from Republicans about faith and religion, while opponents have also targeted aspects of his personal background as they seek to portray him as out of step with Texas voters. During a 2021 speech in the Texas legislature, Talarico said, "God is nonbinary," in pushback against transgender legislation backed by Republicans. The GOP has seized on the comment and plastered it in their advertising, casting him as too progressive. The Democrat routinely touts his Christian faith as the driving force behind his politics. He's been an outspoken advocate for LGBTQ+ rights in Texas. Talarico acknowledged that the comment was "provocative," but told Newsweek in a September 2025 interview that he was just citing what the Bible teaches. "I don't think, theologically speaking, any of my fellow believers would disagree that God is beyond gender. I recognized how I phrased it, probably raised some eyebrows, but the idea that in Christ, in God, there is neither male nor female, that is not coming from me," he said. What Happens Next? With fewer than 50 days remaining until Election Day, the closely watched Senate race is expected to draw millions more in spending as both campaigns battle for support. Texans must register to vote by October 5. Early voting will be held from October 19 through October 30, with Election Day on November 3. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Geoffrey Rowland.
news.summary: The Texas Senate race remains tight, with Paxton trailing Talarico by 3 points in a new poll, within the margin of error.
news.author: Mandy Taheri

news.title: Kamala Harris is to campaign in Michigan with Abdul El-Sayed
news.text:
LANSING, Mich. -- Former Vice President Kamala Harris plans to campaign with Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan next week in the party’s latest push to unify voters in a key battleground state that will help determine control of the Senate.

Harris and El-Sayed have spoken multiple times since she endorsed the progressive Democrat after his primary victory, but this is the first time they’ll appear publicly together.

Harris and El-Sayed will attend a roundtable focused on Black maternal health on Tuesday, according to his campaign spokesperson. El-Sayed is a doctor and the former head of health departments in Detroit and Wayne County.

“Vice President Harris looks forward to returning to Michigan to help turn out the vote in this critical state,” Eduardo Negrón, Harris’ spokesperson, said in a statement. “It is critical we flip the Senate so we can bring down prices and stand up to Donald Trump’s corruption.”

El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers, a former U.S. representative, in November. Republicans have repeatedly attacked El-Sayed, portraying him as the kind of “radical” liberal they say has taken over the Democratic Party.

The seat, currently held by Democrat Gary Peters, is among the must-wins for Democrats as they try to achieve control of the Senate. The party needs to flip four GOP-held seats to take a majority, if Democrats keep the Michigan seat. If Rogers were to flip Michigan to Republicans, the Democrats' challenge would be even greater.

Some other top-ranking Democrats have thrown their weight behind El-Sayed after a bitter primary against Rep. Haley Stevens that highlighted divisions within their party, notably on U.S. support for Israel. In August, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg urged a crowd of hundreds in Detroit to unify behind Democratic candidates in the midterms.

Harris, who lost the 2024 presidential race to Trump, is seen as a possible 2028 candidate. Michigan will be the fifth state to vote in the Democratic presidential primary.

While in Michigan, Harris will also meet with local elected officials and the Rev. Wendell Anthony, the president of the NAACP’s Detroit branch, according to her spokesperson.

GaNun is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

news.title: Explosive Judiciary Committee Report Accuses ActBlue of Major Fraudulent Donation Cover-Up
news.text:
The House Judiciary Committee, along with the House Administration Committee and the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, released an interim staff report on ActBlue, the Democratic fundraising platform.

In that report, the Committees found that ActBlue failed to prevent illegal foreign political contributions, and it's being called an "explosive" insight into the organization's practices.

🚨 BREAKING: Our investigation found that ActBlue weakened fraud safeguards despite detecting significant fraud campaigns, including several from foreign sources.Internal training even told staff to “look for reasons to accept contributions.”Learn more below 👇🏻 pic.twitter.com/iGuqIOuzHP— Oversight Committee (@GOPoversight) September 16, 2026

Two years ago, the Committees began investigating ActBlue's fraud-prevention practices. In 2024, ActBlue changed its fraud policy twice during the presidential campaign, reportedly implementing "more lenient" standards that let foreign donors and other suspicious donor money flow into U.S. campaigns.

Earlier this year, The New York Times reported that the organization's lawyers warned that its chief executive had given potentially misleading responses to Republican investigators. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton filed a suit against the organization over its allowing foreign donations and lying about its donation practices.

10 out of 10 ActBlue employees took the fifth.— Rep. Jim Jordan (@Jim_Jordan) September 16, 2026

When called to testify before Congress, several ActBlue staffers ended up pleading the Fifth, and more recent reporting showed that an elderly Michigan woman made 15,000 donations totaling more than $150,000 to various candidates, including Abdul El-Sayed, through ActBlue. That woman — who lives in a trailer on a fixed income — denied making those donations, although she said she has sent some money to Democrats.

In its report, the Committees found that not only did ActBlue CEO Regina Wallace-Jones may have misled Congress about ActBlue's review process for foreign contributions and that it appeared to be "knowing and willful" in accepting those contributions, but that the organization also engaged in whistleblower retaliation.

You can read the entire report here:

New information obtained by the Committees also showed ActBlue had an "unserious" approach to fraud prevention. This includes failed policies that allegedly "prevent" illegal, fraudulent contributions; a "passport verification process" that was an "ineffective security method" that did not require a valid U.S. passport number; and instructions to fraud prevention analysts to "give the donor the benefit of the doubt" and ignore red flags on donations with foreign indicators.

MORE FRAUD AT ACTBLUE: New information produced to @JudiciaryGOP, @HouseAdmin, and @GOPOversight shows just how unserious ActBlue’s fraud-prevention practices are. Accepting foreign donations in U.S. elections is ILLEGAL.ActBlue knows this, but repeatedly instructed its…— House Judiciary GOP 🇺🇸🇺🇸🇺🇸 (@JudiciaryGOP) September 16, 2026

This means ActBlue employees were often instructed to accept a donation they had previously rejected over signs of being an illegal foreign contribution. One employee said that a donor who "has a few red flags, such as IP/billing mismatch and a concerning IP provider name, a foreign credit card, an odd email domain, and [is] connected to other rejected users via browser fingerprint," should be accepted because ActBlue "can't say for sure that this is fraud." An analyst reported "an odd pattern of small donations to the [Kamala] Harris campaign using prepaid cards." But another ActBlue employee said that donation was "good to accept."

In its conclusion, the report said, "American elections belong to American citizens. ActBlue, one of the largest online political contribution platforms, maintains unserious fraud-prevention practices that allow illegal foreign donations in U.S. elections. The Committees have been conducting oversight ofActBlue’s lax fraud-prevention practices since 2024. This third interim report presents new information about ActBlue’s unserious approach to fraud prevention."

It also noted that "internal logs show how ActBlue maintains a culture that instructs fraud analysts to err on the side of accepting questionable foreign donations."

ActBlue continues to deny any wrongdoing.

This report should send shockwaves through the Democrat Party, because the issue here is bigger than a handful of suspicious donations or a few questionable decisions by fraud analysts. Federal law prohibits foreign nationals from contributing to American elections, and ActBlue, as it moved billions of dollars into political campaigns, had a responsibility to take signs of foreign or fraudulent activity seriously and to follow federal law.

The Committees' investigation alleges that ActBlue repeatedly did the opposite: weakening safeguards, loosening guidelines, giving questionable donors the "benefit of the doubt," and instructing employees to look for reasons to accept contributions even when transactions raised red flags.

Those findings raise a much larger question that Congress, regulators, and ultimately ActBlue itself will have to answer: How much questionable money made it through those safeguards and into American political campaigns? And who will be held accountable for it?

news.title: Reporter's Notebook: House control could hinge on whether the old political rules still apply
news.text: Are we playing with the old playbook or a new playbook in the midterm elections this fall? That’s unclear. It’s hard to determine simply because we’ve seen so much that’s "new" in politics lately. Norms are cast aside. The American system quaked to its core in recent years. You’ve witnessed an American president win the election by prevailing in the Electoral College but losing the popular vote. To have that happen twice in 16 years (2000 and 2016) is astonishing, considering the fact that such an outcome only unfolded on three occasions before. You then had a president impeached twice yet return to office a few years later. There was the Capitol riot as arguing continued about the 2020 election. FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS WANT MAJOR CHANGE AMID ECONOMIC AND POLITICAL DISCONTENT If this is the old playbook, Democrats likely light up the scoreboard in November. The party of the president typically loses about 25 seats in a president’s first midterm. Midterm elections are frequently a referendum on the president. That’s why many Republicans are trying to keep President Donald Trump at arm’s length, considering that his polling numbers are anywhere from the mid-30s to 40% on a good day. Gas prices are high. Grocery prices are skyrocketing. The war in Iran lingers. There’s a trade war with one of America’s best allies. On the old playbook, this portends a disaster for the GOP in this fall’s midterms. But what if we’re using the new playbook? President Trump — and sometimes Republicans aligned with him — have shown a remarkable resilience to defy political gravity and norms. Control of the House could come down to just a few seats. What if there are questions about election security and the validity of who won and lost? There’s redistricting. On paper, Republicans probably redrew about five to six seats nationwide in their favor. If things are tight, we might not know which party wins the House on election night. Perhaps a few days down the road — if not later. That is, unless it’s a Democratic blowout. And remember what we said a few moments ago about the president’s party losing so many seats in that first midterm? Yes, in a way, this is President Trump’s "first midterm." But not really. He experienced a midterm in 2018. Not that things went in the GOP’s favor that year. There’s no contemporary data on how the party of a president might perform after he’s been out of office and rallied to victory a few years later. Also, the sheer reduction by both parties of seats which are in play mitigates political "waves" which crash across the political shoreline in House midterm races. Think 1994 and 2010 for Republicans. 2018 for Democrats. Thus, even though many of the factors favor the Democrats, the possibility remains it could be tough for the party to flip the House. In 2018, the Democrats’ carried an approval rating of 44%. For this time around, it’s 37%. That rivals polling related to the president. In 2018, voters had had enough of President Trump and wanted a change. But because of the polling parity this year, it’s not so obvious that voters are so turned off by President Trump that they automatically gravitate to the Democrats. Here’s another factor: turnout. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: WHAT’S IN AN ECONOMY? President Trump has worked hard to tell voters that he’s "on the ballot" this fall. That cuts two ways. President Trump’s presence on the ballot has historically driven people to the polls. In 2016, 60.1% of registered voters showed up. In 2020, an eye-popping 66.4% of all voters cast ballots. And in 2024, 64.3% of those registered to vote did so. But considering the president’s unpopularity, the cognizance of voters that he’s "on the ballot" could also deter them from turning out. At least those who previously supported him. And those impacts ricochet down to House races. The president’s track record at turning out independent voters in races that count wasn’t great down ballot even as he won the White House in 2024. Consider that, in the 2018 midterms, 50.1% of registered voters materialized. Just 46.1% voted in the 2022 midterms. It was 36.1% in the 2014 midterms — 41% in the historic 2010 midterms where Republicans won a record 63 House seats. This "Trump on the ballot" initiative might not resound with voters. Especially since the president conceded — en route to his midterm convention in Dallas — that gas prices wouldn’t decrease until after the election. He also said the U.S. is stuck with the war in Iran through the midterms. So, how do we know what to anticipate in November? It’s really hard to read if there’s not a clear wave coming. The best way to postulate control of the House is by going race to race. And that is a painstaking process. For instance, will Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, D-Mo., have a district in which to run? Missouri Republicans tried to draw Cleaver out of his district earlier this year. Then a court ruled last week that the Show-Me State must use the old congressional districts, likely meaning that Cleaver was safe. Then another judge ruled that voters already cast ballots in primaries. So, the new maps were back, and Cleaver may be out. All of this less than two months before the election. MISSOURI HIGH COURT BLOCKS GOP-BACKED CONGRESSIONAL MAPS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS; TRUMP BLASTS 'RIDICULOUS' RULING Is there a groundswell for Democrats in Iowa where the Senate seat and governor’s mansion are in jeopardy for Republicans? If that’s the case, Democrats might have a shot of claiming at least two if not three seats there: Republican Iowa Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, Zach Nunn and maybe the seat that Rep. Ashley Hinson is vacating in her quest to become a senator. How about Ohio? There are competitive gubernatorial and Senate contests. Does a Democratic surge boost Rep. Greg Landsman, D-Ohio? Do the accusations of spousal and child abuse bounce embattled Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio., in what is otherwise a relatively safe Republican seat? Rep. Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, clung to her seat by fewer than 1,000 votes two years ago. But that was when President Trump carried the Buckeye State by 11 points and Kaptur’s district. Redistricting actually turned Kaptur’s turf slightly more in her favor. But the 80-year-old Kaptur was in a car wreck in August, inhibiting her ability to campaign. Is that a factor? How well do Democrats perform in Virginia? Rep. Jen Kiggans, R-Va., faces former Rep. Elaine Luria, D-Va., who she vanquished in 2022. Could former Rep. Tom Perriello, D-Va., who won in a 2008 upset in a differently-drawn district and promptly lost in 2010, unseat Rep. John McGuire, R-Va.? Rep. Jared Golden, D-Maine, is retiring. Former Republican Maine Gov. Paul LePage is running for Golden’s seat. Does LePage benefit from Democratic chaos in the effort to unseat Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine? After all, President Trump won one of Maine’s three electoral votes in 2024, capturing that congressional district over former Vice President Kamala Harris. We could bounce around the map, district to district, all day like this. But sans a wave, that’s what you must do to properly filet the House races. Most conventional arrows point in the direction of Democrats winning the House this fall. Yet it probably shouldn’t be this close. That’s why you have to go by the playbook. news.summary: Trump's mid-30s approval and high gas prices favor Democrats, but redistricting and turnout questions could keep House races razor-tight.

news.title: Kamala Harris is to campaign in Michigan with Abdul El-Sayed
news.text:
LANSING, Mich. (AP) — Former Vice President Kamala Harris plans to campaign with Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan next week in the party’s latest push to unify voters in a key battleground state that will help determine control of the Senate.

Harris and El-Sayed have spoken multiple times since she endorsed the progressive Democrat after his primary victory, but this is the first time they’ll appear publicly together.

Harris and El-Sayed will attend a roundtable focused on Black maternal health on Tuesday, according to his campaign spokesperson. El-Sayed is a doctor and the former head of health departments in Detroit and Wayne County.

“Vice President Harris looks forward to returning to Michigan to help turn out the vote in this critical state,” Eduardo Negrón, Harris’ spokesperson, said in a statement. “It is critical we flip the Senate so we can bring down prices and stand up to Donald Trump’s corruption.”

El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers, a former U.S. representative, in November. Republicans have repeatedly attacked El-Sayed, portraying him as the kind of “radical” liberal they say has taken over the Democratic Party.

The seat, currently held by Democrat Gary Peters, is among the must-wins for Democrats as they try to achieve control of the Senate. The party needs to flip four GOP-held seats to take a majority, if Democrats keep the Michigan seat. If Rogers were to flip Michigan to Republicans, the Democrats' challenge would be even greater.

Some other top-ranking Democrats have thrown their weight behind El-Sayed after a bitter primary against Rep. Haley Stevens that highlighted divisions within their party, notably on U.S. support for Israel. In August, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg urged a crowd of hundreds in Detroit to unify behind Democratic candidates in the midterms.

Harris, who lost the 2024 presidential race to Trump, is seen as a possible 2028 candidate. Michigan will be the fifth state to vote in the Democratic presidential primary.

While in Michigan, Harris will also meet with local elected officials and the Rev. Wendell Anthony, the president of the NAACP’s Detroit branch, according to her spokesperson.

news.title: LinkedIn Co-Founder Reid Hoffman Says Harris Would Face ‘Very Challenging Path’ in 2028
news.text:
LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman said on Sept. 16 that former Vice President Kamala Harris would face a difficult road if she runs for president again in 2028.

Hoffman was asked whether Harris, a Democrat, should run during an onstage interview at Politico’s Decoded Summit in Washington.

“I think it would be a very challenging path for her, and it’s going to be a very noisy field,” Hoffman said.

Hoffman, a partner at the venture capital firm Greylock, is one of the Democratic Party’s largest individual donors, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) records. He backed President Joe Biden’s reelection bid and then Harris’s 2024 campaign after she replaced Biden at the top of the ticket.

FEC records show that he gave at least $10.25 million to Future Forward PAC, the main super PAC supporting the Democratic ticket in 2024. That total includes $10 million before Biden withdrew in July and $250,000 in October, after Harris became the Democratic nominee.

Hoffman’s largest single contribution on record came on June 30, when he gave $10 million to Lone Star Rising PAC, a super PAC backing James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Texas. FEC records show Hoffman has given the group $11.5 million since January.

He has also given $310,000 to the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and $310,100 to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, FEC records show.

“I don’t know if she runs, but we'll see,” Newsom said. “I wouldn’t run if she ran.”

Newsom said a primary between the two Californians would help their opponents and split the same base of voters.

“First of all, electorally, it’s a gift from God for everybody else. They'd enjoy the hell out of it. Mutual assured destruction. It services no greater good,” he said. “I know her base of supporters, I know her friends, the Venn diagram on that is just pure crossover. I wouldn’t do that to people.”

At the same Politico event on Wednesday, Hoffman was asked whether he would support Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) if she became the Democratic nominee. He did not rule it out.

“Well, it depends a little bit on, I mean, I think she’s much more pragmatic than people give her credit for,” Hoffman said. “It depends on who she’s running against.”

Hoffman said his support generally comes down to two questions.

“I tend to be, if you’re basically kind of pro-society, which she is, and pro-business, which is a question, that tends to be where I think the right focal points are,” he said.

Asked whether she might instead challenge Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), she said, “Anything is possible at this juncture.”

When queried about Harris, Hoffman first joked that it was “the thing you want to ask the tech guy on AI.”

The interviewer responded that “all of the tech policy is going to be downstream from whoever gets [the presidential nomination].”

The Epoch Times has reached out to Harris’s office and Ocasio-Cortez’s office for comment.
news.summary: Hoffman also said Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is ‘much more pragmatic than people give her credit for.’

news.title: Arkansas Democrat Hallie Shoffner: ‘We’d Trade Five Americans’ for One ‘Undocumented Immigrant’
news.text:
Hallie Shoffner, who is running to unseat Sen. Tom Cotton (R-AR), defended “undocumented” farm workers as exceptionally hardworking, after previously saying she grew up around “undocumented” farm workers, discussing Mexican H-2A employees on her family farm, defending farmers’ reliance on foreign-born labor, and leading a nonprofit that assisted “undocumented Hispanics.”

“Every farmer will tell you at one point, we did, or still do, employ undocumented immigrants, and it’s absolutely ridiculous that these folks are being rounded up because they’re hardworking people,” Shoffner said on Free Arkansas with host Andy McNeill. “They’re some of the best people we know, and honestly, we’d trade five Americans for just one of them because of how hard they work.”

“And why is it that there’s no pathway for them to work here legally when they’re good workers? We pay them well. They spend money here. They have family here,” Shoffner said.

“We’re acting like all Republicans like what’s happening with ICE, and Tom Cotton’s basically saying you, Andy, if you’re a Republican and you disagree with my position on ICE, or if you’re asking any kind of questions about it, well, you must be anti-American and anti-safety,” Shoffner said. “And I’m like, I have a seven-year-old boy. All I think about is safety.”

Laura Loomer highlighted the interview on X, writing, “The facts are clear: Farmer Hallie loves putting illegal aliens first, which is why she is UNFIT to serve in the U.S. Senate.”

In a report on Loomered, Loomer also pointed to a portion of the interview in which host Andy McNeill questioned why ICE agents needed to dress like “SEAL Team Six.” Shoffner responded that the use of bulletproof vests “seems kind of performative to me.”

In June, Shoffner said immigrants “whether they have documents or not” are essential to the country’s “social, cultural, and economic fabric” and contribute to the small-business economy. Shoffner was then asked whether she would vote to defund ICE and answered, “I would vote to defund ICE as it exists right now.” She said the agency no longer served its original purpose and that she “would not spend one more dime on ICE,” before pointing to hunger among Arkansas children as an issue she would address.

Shoffner later denied wanting to defund the agency, writing in response to Cotton, “I don’t want to defund ICE. I want to reform it.” During an Arkansas television interview, an anchor asked Shoffner about an ad claiming that she wanted more illegal immigrants in the country, wanted to abolish immigration law enforcement, and had given to Kamala Harris 25 times. When the anchor asked whether she had said those things, Shoffner answered, “No.”

Shoffner’s connection to immigrant communities predates her Senate campaign. She previously served as executive director of Seis Puentes, a Little Rock nonprofit focused on the Latino community. In 2012, she told the Arkansas Times that one of the organization’s goals was helping “undocumented Hispanics” navigate American systems and “engage them in the process.” Seis Puentes also partnered with North Little Rock to help illegal immigrants obtain “valid photo ID.”

Shoffner also said she “grew up in an immigrant community” and that “the farm workers for all the farms… were generally from Mexico and Honduras” during a January 2026 podcast interview. “Many of them were undocumented, but their children… were U.S. citizens or Dreamers. And so I learned Spanish,” she said.

She has repeatedly defended foreign agricultural labor as important to Arkansas farms. In a September 2025 interview, she described the H-2A program as “how farmers get labor” and said the country had “gotten ourselves into a situation where we rely on foreign-born labor.” She asked, “What if we build an immigration system where we actually went to these farmers and went to these employers and asked what they need as opposed to just blanket policies that make it so that we can’t get affordable labor?”

Shoffner has criticized Department of Homeland Security inspections of housing for H-2A agricultural workers. In August 2025, Shoffner said Arkansas farms use the H-2A Agricultural Visa Program to recruit foreign-born workers from Mexico and South Africa. “Now the Department of Homeland Security has suddenly decided it’s their job to inspect H-2A Visa housing,” she said.

She questioned why the inspections were taking place, adding, “My only thinking is they don’t want farmers to access labor, they don’t want farmers to be successful, they don’t want farmers to grow food, and we are going to be a country reliant on others to feed us.”

Beyond immigration, Shoffner has connected agriculture to climate change. In 2020, she called climate change a threat to “my business, my way of life, and the legacy I will leave for my son: the farm.” Shoffner said “emissions-driven climate change amplifies extreme weather events,” including “longer droughts, more torrential rains, and stronger storms,” and stated that farmers could face “more challenging seasons jeopardizing our ability to make a profitable crop.”

She criticized the Trump administration and the Department of Government Efficiency over changes to agricultural programs. In an April 2025 post, she listed “Farm to school programs (cancelled by DOGE), SNAP access at farmers markets (cancelled by DOGE), Local processing facilities (threatened by tariffs), Support for women- and BIPOC-owned farms (cancelled by Trump),” which she described as part of “the true path to health in rural America.”

Shoffner has also focused on race in her agricultural advocacy. Discussing three black farmers in a 2024 profile, Shoffner said, “As a society, we pretty much did everything possible to ensure that Black farmers did not become prosperous farm families.” She added that “women and minority farmers who live on the margins of the industry at large are deserving of a first shot at the specialty rice industry.”

In another statement, Shoffner described herself as a beneficiary of advantages she said were historically unavailable to black farmers. “As a white multi-generational farmer, I know the privilege that propelled our family to success, although ours was modest compared to others,” she said. Shoffner described this as “a privilege not given to black farmers systematically disenfranchised of their livelihoods and their land and murdered for standing up for what they believe in.”

Shoffner has also framed programs supporting women and smaller farming operations in terms of diversity, equity, and inclusion. In a January, 2025 LinkedIn post, she wrote, “As a woman farmer running a small farm, I have been fortunate to participate in programs that support smaller operations like mine.” She added, “These initiatives enable me to access opportunities that our farm’s size would typically hinder,” before concluding, “This is diversity, equity, and inclusion in action.”

Hallie Shoffner, who is running to unseat Sen.
