news.title: Trump stumps for Senate candidate in North Carolina as Republicans fear losing seat
news.text:
President Donald Trump is making his first campaign trip since he rallied Republicans at the party's midterm convention -- stumping for North Carolina Senate candidate Michael Whatley, whose race could decide control of Congress in November.

The seat would typically be a comfortable bet for the GOP -- North Carolina hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008, and Trump won the state in the past three presidential elections. But economic pain is hitting the state hard, which could impact the race.

The president's visit to Gastonia, North Carolina -- just outside the Charlotte metro area -- comes as polls show Whatley, the former chair of the Republican National Committee, continues to trail behind former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat elected statewide in North Carolina six times, in a race that has seen millions in cash poured into it.

Doug Heye, a Republican strategist and former communications director for the RNC, said he always thought this year's Senate race in North Carolina, replacing retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, would be "tough" for Republicans. North Carolina's Senate race is among several crucial races for control of the upper chamber where Republican have a narrow majority.

As prices continue to go up from the gas pump to the grocery store aisle, experts say North Carolinians' concerns over affordability are dominating the conversation on the ground -- and Whatley could end up bearing the brunt of those frustrations at the ballot box.

"The No. 1 thing people are talking about is what they just spent, whether that's at the gas station or at the grocery store or at a restaurant," said Heye, a North Carolina native who has spent time in the state this year.

Dr. Susan Roberts, a political science professor at nearby Davidson College, says that most voters are going to consider the cost of living when deciding who to vote for in November.

"I don't think it's going to be a referendum on Trump, as it is a referendum on the economy -- and what Trump might have wrought,” Roberts said.

Cooper has branded his latest campaign swing as a "Make Stuff Cost Less" tour, as North Carolina Democrats work to tie Whatley -- a close Trump ally who led the North Carolina GOP before taking up the mantle at the RNC -- to the rise in prices that voters have experienced over the course of Trump's second term in office.

David Brown, the chair of the local Democratic Party, says that Trump's visit to his county comes as high costs are "eating into everybody's budgets."

"He's coming at a time when we're seeing all these record gas prices from his Iran war," Brown said.

Some Republicans -- as well as the White House -- have argued that policies passed by the Biden administration are the reason for the rising costs across the country, but Heye notes that in American politics, "the president who's in power is the one who gets the credit or the blame" on the economy.

The Whatley campaign is eager to welcome the president to Gaston County, where Trump defeated Kamala Harris by more than 20 points in 2024.

"No one fires up Republicans to get out and vote like President Trump does and his visit is an important part of turning out Republicans to the polls this November," Whatley campaign spokesperson DJ Griffin told ABC News in a statement.

Heye noted that Trump has historically driven turnout, but only when Trump is on the ballot.

"There is a drop off when it's not him,” he said, before adding that Trump also tends to drive turnout among Democrats as well.

At the Republican Midterm Convention last week, Trump told Republicans to "pretend that I'm on the ballot."

“When I'm on the ticket, Republicans always do very well ...," Trump said. "So I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot. I'm on the ballot. I'm on the -- just one more time."

The Cooper campaign characterized the president's visit to the state as a bail-out attempt from "Whatley's D.C. insider friends" -- adding in a statement that Cooper is the "only candidate with plans to make stuff cost less."

Jay Berry, a small business owner in nearby Lincolnton whose manufacturing company has contracts with the government, says that even though gas prices have gone up, he’s glad the president is visiting.

"Everybody loves President Trump," he said.

But Berry said he won’t be attending Wednesday's event, telling ABC News that he has heard enough campaign speeches and already believes that Whatley will be a "better leader" than Cooper.

“I don’t need to go see the cow, knowing that’s what I’m going to buy."
news.summary: Experts say Michael Whatley could bear the brunt of voters' economic frustrations.

news.title: Two-thirds of Americans say Trump is wrong and AI could destroy humanity, poll finds
news.text:
A new poll has found that a majority of Americans believe AI could pose a threat to humanity, despite President Donald Trump playing down the risks.

The new Politico poll found that even a majority of Republican voters believe that AI poses a potential risk to the survival of the human race. 

According to the online survey of 2,064 people, 70 percent of those who voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 thought there was either a moderate risk (29 percent), significant risk (24 percent) or an almost certainty (17 percent) of AI destroying humanity. Some 21 percent said there was either a small risk (14 percent) or no risk at all (7 percent), while the rest said they didn’t know.

Of Trump voters, 61 percent thought there was either a moderate risk (27 percent), a significant risk (17 percent) or an almost certainty (17 percent) of AI ending human existence, while 20 percent thought the risk very low, 9 percent thought there was no risk, and 10 percent said they didn’t know.

Overall, 63 percent of respondents thought there was either a moderate risk (26 percent), a significant risk (20 percent), or a near certainty (17 percent), with 15 percent saying the risk was very small, 7 percent saying no risk at all and 15 percent saying they didn’t know.

The survey comes days after Trump himself rejected the idea of any deliberate slowdown in the development of AI following warnings from those working in the industry that the technology could get out of hand. In an unusual move, some of the leading pioneers of AI – including Sam Altman of OpenAI, Dario Amodei of Anthropic and Elon Musk of xAI – suggested they were sympathetic to slowing down development.

Last week Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic researcher, claimed he had quit the company because those building AI are "gambling with our lives" and that they “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

His resignation and subsequent cable news interviews kicked off a debate over whether the threat is real, or – as some critics suggested – marketing hype, or efforts by the big AI companies to slow down rivals by introducing new regulations.

Trump reacted by claiming any suggestion of AI being a threat was a "hoax" and comparing it to global warming and some of the accusations he has faced during his political career.

"I am the Hoax Buster, and I’m right now breaking another Hoax — That AI is going to take over, consume, and destroy the World, and that Robots will be marching into our Cities, and getting rid of us all! This is even wilder than the RUSSIA, RUSSIA, RUSSIA HOAX, or the Global Warming Scam. Thank you for your attention to this matter! President DONALD J. TRUMP," he wrote on Tuesday. 

The president also said that he was himself the only “guardrail” that the emerging technology required, writing: “The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!"

Trump also warned that major restrictions on AI development in the U.S. could hand the initiative to rivals in China. He wrote: “Don’t kill the Golden Goose.”

Several recent incidents involving AI have appeared to prove that the technology can act independently from human oversight. In July OpenAI admitted that an experimental version of ChatGPT had gone rogue and attacked another AI company.

In Congress, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have said action is needed to monitor how AI develops.

Some Democrats are reportedly considering the creation of a House select committee on AI should they be able to take back control of the House following the midterm elections. Senator Bernie Sanders, who has frequently called for reforms in the AI industry to protect American jobs and health, claimed that what he called Trump’s ignorance about AI was “truly embarrassing.” 

“Congress under both Democratic and Republican control has been asleep at the wheel,”he said during the the Pro-Human Assembly in D.C. on Tuesday. “And we now have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing.”

On the GOP side, Senator John Kennedy proposed a bill to force AI developers to include a “kill switch” in their programs.

Meanwhile, other issues related to AI are continuing to concern Americans. A survey by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago found that 53 percent of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the environmental effects of AI data centers. That figure is up from 41 percent a year ago.

Michael Greenstone, who directs the University of Chicago institute which collaborated on the survey, said: “We’re undertaking a massive experiment in real time, and I don’t think there’ll be any putting the milk back in the bottle. Change is scary, and I think some of that is being reflected here.”

Gallup found in May that 7 out of 10 Americans oppose data centers being built in their towns. 

Senator Chris Murphy, a Democrat, has been critical of free-rein AI development, and said he recognizes that fears over AI is a "dominant issue" for voters. 

“We have to stop AI from poisoning our kids, our culture, and destroying millions of jobs,” he told Politico. “This is an immediate crisis, Donald Trump has made it clear where he stands with the AI companies, and the Democratic Party has to put this question to the electorate this November.”
news.summary: Seventy percent of people who voted Democrat in 2024 and 60 percent of people who voted Republican agree that AI poses a potential risk to the survival of the human race

news.title: Map of Trump Approval Rating in Biggest Farming States as Diesel Costs Soar
news.text: President Donald Trump’s approval rating is underwater in the nation’s largest farm states as diesel prices have surged in recent days, a major warning sign for Republicans ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. Rising diesel prices could have critical impacts for farmers, who rely on diesel to power agricultural equipment. Rising prices could also drive up transportation costs across the agricultural industry. Rising diesel prices stem from disruptions to oil and fuel shipments in the Middle East amid the United States' war in Iran, which began earlier this year. Why It Matters For Republicans, there is a political risk if farmers, a core part of the Republican base that helped elect Trump in 2016 and 2024, abandon the party or sit out the midterms due to frustration over the impact. Diesel also powers trucks, trains and ships that move agricultural products across the supply chain, increasing transportation costs across the industry. Some farmers have criticized Trump amid rising diesel prices. Democrats are increasingly hopeful about their chances of flipping the state this year in both the Senate and gubernatorial races. In the Senate race, polls show a toss-up between Democratic state Representative James Talarico and Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, while Republican Governor Greg Abbott is viewed as the favorite against Democratic state Representative Gina Hinojosa in the gubernatorial race. Trump was 18 points underwater, with 38 percent approving of his job performance and 56 percent disapproving, according to Civiqs. In 2024, the state backed Trump by nearly 14 points over Harris. Nebraska In Nebraska, Trump’s approval rating was 5 points in the negative, with 43 percent approving and 48 percent disapproving, according to Civiqs. Nebraska voted for Trump by nearly 20 points in 2024. The Senate race is viewed as being potentially competitive. Republican Senator Pete Ricketts faces a challenge from independent Dan Osborn, and some polls suggest a competitive race. Minnesota Trump’s approval was -35 points in Minnesota, where 28 percent of respondents approved of him, and 63 percent disapproved, according to Civiqs. Harris won Minnesota by about 4 points in 2024. Republicans hope to make the state competitive this year, but polling and forecasts show Democrats Amy Klobuchar and Peggy Flanagan leading Republicans Lisa Demuth and Michelle Tafoya in the gubernatorial and Senate races, respectively. "The notion that I think the president and I share is that we should let the race play out, that the risk of global extinction is not real, it is in fact a hoax," Will Thibeau, a former Palantir deployment strategist who later worked in the Pentagon’s Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office, told Fox News Digital. TRUMP UNLOADS ON TECH TITANS PUSHING FOR SLOWDOWN ON EMERGING INDUSTRY: ‘WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!’ "The stakes of losing to China, of losing the opportunity to transform our economy, are so high that we shouldn't let 'doomerism' define public policy," the retired Army Ranger added. Thibeau’s position is not that Washington should take a hands-off approach to AI, but that the U.S. should race aggressively at the frontier while narrowly addressing concrete risks — threading the needle between denying China an advantage and preventing regulations backed by today’s leading AI firms from entrenching a "duopoly" at the expense of new American innovators. Enhanced manufacturing capabilities, enhanced processing power, decision-making in financial markets," he said, disputing the idea that Beijing will not race full bore because the technology could countervail the CCP’s grip by incidentally empowering civilians. LET CONGRESS DECIDE WHAT COMES NEXT Those "hyperventilating" over either extreme, he argued, miss the "clearly defined middle path" for AI development. While Thibeau said fears of "drone swarms run amok" are not realistic, he acknowledged AI carries real risks that policymakers should address without allowing those concerns to justify sweeping rules that slow U.S. development or undermine its military edge. The larger danger, he argued, is that leading AI firms can absorb regulations that smaller newcomers cannot. "There is a duopoly, perhaps a triopoly if you include Google," Thibeau said, naming Anthropic and OpenAI as the two companies clearly in the lead. news.title: Trump on the ballot: Will it help Republicans?
news.text:
At last week’s GOP convention, President Donald Trump told the enthusiastic crowd he had a problem. He told them that when he’s not on the ballot, they say his people don’t show up in big numbers to vote for other Republicans, putting their majorities in the House and Senate in jeopardy. He followed that up by imploring his supporters, “I’m asking you to pretend that I’m on the ballot … just one more time.” 

With that, Trump made the upcoming midterm elections all about him. Was it a sound strategic decision made by Trump and his team? Was it simply a nod to the reality that midterms, historically, are a reflection of voters’ view of the sitting president and the job he is doing? Or in this case, given Trump’s sinking job approval, an attempt to make the best out of a challenging situation?

This election is all about Trump, and he seems fine with that. But will a focus on the president rather than congressional Republicans’ legislative record help or hurt their chances?

There are two ways to look at it. First, analyzing previous elections, how did Republican candidates do with Trump on the ballot versus when he was not? Second, how will his job approval numbers affect the election outcome? 

The critical element in Trump’s win in 2024 was his ability to carry all seven presidential battleground states. In five of those seven states, however, there was also a U.S. Senate race on the ballot: Arizona, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Out of those five races, only one Republican managed a win, Dave McCormick, who squeaked out a 0.2-point victory in Pennsylvania. 

The four GOP losing candidates were facing better Democratic candidates who ran better campaigns than the Democratic nominee, Vice President Kamala Harris. But, more important, McCormick was the only candidate of the five who won independents, in this case, by a 3-point margin. 

As an aside, one might also wonder how Harris lost four competitive states where Democratic Senate candidates won. 

In the last two elections, we saw that House races weren’t immune from this political dichotomy. In 2022, House Republicans won 222 seats. In 2024, with Trump on the ballot, they won 220. This was despite voter unhappiness with President Joe Biden’s economic policies. Exit polls found that 75 percent of the electorate said inflation caused a moderate or severe hardship to them or their families. Yet Republicans lost two seats.

A look back at previous elections provides some insight into the impact of presidential job approval on midterm elections. Over the past three decades, the House majority has flipped five times — in 1994, 2006, 2010, 2018 and 2022. In each of those elections, the incumbent president’s party lost the House; and in every case, the sitting president’s job approval was underwater. 

Across those five, exit polls showed the presidential job approval ranged from 43 percent to 45 percent. The disapproval ranged from 52 percent to 57 percent. The best of those was Trump in 2018 (45-54) and the worst was George W. Bush in 2006 (43-57). What should be most concerning for the Trump team today is how much lower his approval is than previous presidents’ ratings. 

Trump’s job approval, according to the Real Clear Politics average, has been underwater since mid-March of 2025. On Tuesday, his current RCP average job approval overall was 40 percent, while 57 percent disapprove.

The president’s economic numbers, which are the most important to voters, particularly inflation, reflect Republicans’ biggest challenge. His job approval on the economy is 35-61, and on inflation, 29-68, according to the RCP average.

To buck history, Trump needs to overcome voter dissatisfaction with the economy. That will take an environment where voters can walk into a grocery store or fill up their cars believing that “I am better able now to handle these prices.” 

Given voters’ current view of the economy, that’s a tall order. There is no doubt that Republicans have slipped since the November 2024 election. Fortunately, while voters may be unhappy with the economy, they also don’t believe Democrats have produced any real policies to put the economy back on track. Democrats have talked a lot about affordability but have offered only dated and demonstrably ineffective solutions to improve the economy. 

People understand that somebody has to pay for free stuff, whether it’s child care, college, health care or groceries. Hyperbole isn’t a strategy any more than hope and tired promises voters have heard before.

But the same holds true for the other side. Voters aren’t likely to be persuaded by the president’s surprise $5,000 promise to every American adult if the GOP retains control of the House and Senate. Covid checks didn’t win Trump reelection.

Republicans need a closing argument based on more than “Trump is on the ballot.” It’s true that presidential elections turn out more voters than off-year elections, but increased participation doesn’t guarantee victory. 

The vote for congressional House Republicans increased by 20 million votes from 2022 to 2024, yet Republicans lost two seats. Still, a bigger Republican turnout in the midterm this fall could make a difference, especially in Senate races. 

Whether the “Trump on the ballot” strategy will drive enough GOP voters who usually don’t go to the polls in midterms to eke out a victory remains to be seen. 

Voters need a sense of economic direction without the hype, a realistic discussion that acknowledges their concerns and offers real world solutions. People do not believe this is the best economy ever. Telling them otherwise without context or empathy only reinforces the view of many that too many political leaders are disconnected from the experiences of average Americans.

Biden is a perfect example. He tried telling voters how they should feel as he claimed economic progress that people simply weren’t experiencing. Republicans can point to some clear markers of progress and they should. Much of what was in the Big Beautiful Bill has been lost on most voters. Research shows people support the bill when they understand its provisions, from preventing a major income tax increase by making permanent the doubling of the standard deduction and keeping the child tax credit, among others. 

If Republicans want to make history this fall, they need to make a better case for Republican policies because, as the president said at a rally in August, “Our country’s on the ballot.”

David Winston is the president of The Winston Group and a longtime adviser to congressional Republicans. He previously served as the director of planning for Speaker Newt Gingrich. He advises Fortune 100 companies, foundations and nonprofit organizations on strategic planning and public policy issues, as well as serving as an election analyst for CBS News.

news.title: Exclusive: Warren backs pause on AI
news.text:
Driving the news: Warren on Wednesday will call for a pause on advanced AI development but will stop short of calling for a ban on superintelligence, breaking with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.).

"We should immediately press pause on the development of advanced AI while lawmakers and regulators put systems in place to keep people safe," Warren will say ahead of a roundtable hosted by Sanders on Wednesday. "Congress must urgently pass legislation to put stronger guardrails in place before we have a cyberattack, economic crisis, or national security disaster facilitated by AI."Sanders' proposal calls for a pause and a ban on superintelligence, and threatens up to 20 years in prison for violations, which its authors note is similar to the penalties for illegally developing nuclear weapons. 

Between the lines: The progressive movement — like every other political faction — does not have a unified position when it comes to the nitty-gritty of AI regulation. 

Warren and Sanders have also released AI tax plans with varying approaches. Warren has proposed taxing AI companies, while Sanders wants the government to take equity stakes in them.

Catch up quick: Frontier lab CEOs have coalesced around a message of pacing or slowing frontier AI development and seeking international collaboration. 

Warren said the industry's push to "pace the frontier" is "insufficient," arguing that elected officials, not AI CEOs, should decide the technology's future. Suggestions to weaken antitrust protections to confront AI risks are "transparently self-serving," she said.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for an exemption in antitrust law to help coordinate AI pacing. Former antitrust government officials say that would not be necessary because the law does not prevent AI companies from coordinating to prevent harm and sharing legitimate cybersecurity information.

The big picture: More Democrats with national profiles are weighing in on the idea of a pause as the Trump administration flatly rejects it. 

Kamala Harris this week endorsed slowing down and called on President Trump to pursue a treaty with China.Barack Obama also backed the idea of slowing down as a good first step. 

The bottom line: More Democrats are calling to slow AI development, but there's little agreement on what government should do about it.

news.title: The Anti-AI Movement Just Got a TIME Cover and Readers Weren’t Told the Full Story
news.text:
The AI doomerism movement has found its latest magazine cover. 

For its Oct. 12 issue, TIME is sounding the alarm with “The AI Tipping Point,” a cover story from Harry Booth, Naomi Nix and Billy Perrigo that imagines a future in which AI begins improving itself, accelerates beyond anyone’s ability to manage it and is effectively able to outthink, outpace and overpower humanity. Beyond outlining real concerns, the article folds them into a worst-case hypothetical designed to stoke fear about a technology most Americans are only beginning to understand, leaving readers to conclude that a sprawling federal regulatory regime is the only responsible response.

But there is a catch TIME reportedly left out. Booth and Perrigo are affiliated with the Tarbell Center, a journalism fellowship program tied to the effective-altruism network supported by Facebook co-founder and Kamala Harris megadonor Dustin Moskovitz. That same network is preparing to pour more than $1 billion into AI safety, policy and advocacy in 2026. The movement funding the push for AI alarmism is helping supply the journalists writing the headlines, and TIME reportedly did not tell its readers. 

Two of the reporters on the byline are funded by the Tarbell Center, an AI doomer org controlled by Kamala Harris megadonor Dustin Moskovitz. Tarbell gives journalists large grants to insert AI doomer stories into prominent outlets. @TIME did not disclose the affiliation. https://t.co/m3iFoQPUW9— Jordan Schachtel (@JordanSchachtel) September 15, 2026

This comes as other prominent voices in the latest anti-AI panic campaign have also faced questions about their ties to the same billionaire-funded ecosystem. Jacob Coxon, the former Anthropic researcher who publicly resigned last week while warning that AI could become uncontrollable, received a $20,000 scholarship in 2022 from Good Ventures’ “Long-Term Future Scholarship Program.” also a project of Dustin Moskovitz.

None of this necessarily means the concerns about AI are unfounded. But it does mean the public should pay close attention to the incentives behind the panic. Nearly every voice demanding that “something must be done” seems to arrive at the same predetermined destination: a new regulatory agency, new federal mandates and more red tape. All before anyone stops to ask whether existing laws already address genuine misconduct, whether the apocalyptic predictions are grounded in reality, or whether the companies and activists pushing hardest for regulation stand to benefit from a government-built monopoly around the industry.

The cover of Time magazine in 2006 and 2026. From "climate change will destroy humanity" to "AI will destroy humanity". pic.twitter.com/d59DCbTQFi— Dr. Eli David (@DrEliDavid) September 16, 2026

The hope for humanity, and especially for conservatives, should remain grounded in the hope inherent in free markets: confidence in the balancing forces of competition; confidence that profit, reputation and self-preservation give AI companies every reason to prevent catastrophic outcomes; and confidence in humanity’s enduring ability to adapt when new technologies create new challenges. America has confronted disruptive technologies before, adjusted to them and emerged stronger. There is no reason to assume artificial intelligence must be the exception, unless we let fear and bureaucratic ambition make it one.

news.title: The future of AI depends on Donald Trump, says ex-national security adviser
news.text:
A former national security adviser has given a stark warning that any hope for proper global regulation of AI will depend on decisions made by the US.

The UK is doing “groundbreaking” work on the security and safety of artificial intelligence. But the response will depend on other parts of the world, said Jonathan Black, who helped to organise the world’s first global summit on artificial intelligence safety in 2023.

The Bletchley Park summit brought industry leaders like Elon Musk and CEOs from OpenAI and Anthropic together with world leaders from Europe, the US, and China.

Guests included Rishi Sunak, Kamala Harris, and Chinese vice-minister of science and technology Wu Zhaohui. At the end of the summit, 28 countries signed the Bletchley Declaration, calling for global co-operation to collectively manage the risks and responsibilities of artificial intelligence.

Three years is a long time in politics – and even longer in AI. How has this collectivist approach fared since Bletchley Park? Mr Black reflects that while the summit was ‘groundbreaking’, much of the future of artificial intelligence now lies in the hands of the US and China.

“The UK has a lot to be proud of in terms of AI. We’ve been very ahead of the curve. The UK institute has become the most globally recognised for checking that these models are safe,” he said on the In The Room podcast. 

“But quite a lot of this is gonna come down to what the Chinese and the Americans sort out between themselves.”

Fears around a potential existential risk to humanity from artificial intelligence have been supercharged in the last week following calls from Sam Altman and Elon Musk to ‘slow down’ AI development over safety concerns.

Donald Trump responded with a Truth Social rant, branding the concerns a “sick conspiracy” against artificial intelligence and data centres which would only benefit China. 

He railed against the suggestion of any AI governance, insisting that the only guardrail needed is “a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.

“WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!”

China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun dismissed narratives of threat, confrontation, and malicious competition, saying: “All parties should work together to advance AI in a manner that is open, inclusive, beneficial to all, and oriented toward the good.”

Mr Black remains optimistic despite the warnings, fears, and conflicting tones between the two countries he considers industry superpowers. “Those real existential risks matter a lot: that 0.1% [chance] of, you know, are the bots gonna kill us? It's not in America or China’s interest for those things to happen.

“But [regulation] is going to be quite hard to do in practice unless the US government is able to put some sort of rules behind it.

“We should be worried,” Mr Black says. “But we also need to worry about harnessing the benefits.”

Listen to the full episode of In The Room on Apple Podcasts and Spotify, or watch on YouTube.
news.summary: The UK is doing ‘groundbreaking’ work on AI safety – but the risk all depends on what the US and and China decide, says Jonathan Black

news.title: Progressives launch new push to reject campaign money from AI industry
news.text:
Nearly a dozen Democratic congressional candidates are banding together to call on campaigns to refuse money from a major pro-artificial intelligence super PAC ahead of the November midterms.

The new pledge targets Leading the Future, a bipartisan organization that has raised at least $140 million since it launched last year. Its financial supporters include the likes of OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman, Trump-aligned Palantir co-founder Joe Lonsdale and the creators of venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz.

The initiative, first reported by MS NOW, comes at a time of heightened scrutiny of AI’s risks to society and national security after pleas from an Anthropic whistleblower who went public with safety concerns.Signatories to the effort, organized by an anti-OpenAI group called QuitGPT, argue that the political action committee is lobbying to prevent comprehensive AI legislation from passing Congress. The super PAC says it intends to “reshape the political environment around innovation policy” by supporting politicians from both parties who align with their approach and opposing those who do not. 

In response to a request for comment, Josh Vlasto, a former Chuck Schumer staffer who helps lead the super PAC, referred to previous statements by the organization. “We will continue supporting policymakers and candidates who move beyond ideological extremes to advance responsible innovation, protect the public, and strengthen American leadership,” one X post reads.

Rep. Greg Casar of Texas, who chairs the Progressive Caucus, Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts, Rep. Pat Ryan and House candidate Brad Lander, both of New York, former Virginia Rep. Tom Perriello, and California House candidate Angela Gonzales-Torres are among 10 Democratic hopefuls committing to the vow.“In the fight between AI billionaires and the people they're screwing over, Democrats need to stand clearly on the side of the people,” Casar said in a statement. “We must reject support from the billionaires trying to stop all AI regulation.”There is a long list of more than 50 left-leaning organizations that also support the campaign to disavow the super PAC, including the Sunrise Movement, the Generation Z advocacy group Voters of Tomorrow, the liberal activist group Indivisible and End Citizens United, which backs campaign finance reform.

In a sign of friction over the Democratic Party’s path forward, Morris Katz, an adviser to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and other prominent Democrats, took aim at former Vice President Kamala Harris on Tuesday for praising an effort by the venture capital fund SV Angel to strengthen ties between Democrats and AI companies as “encouraging.” Tech investor Ron Conway of SV Angel was one of Leading the Future’s earliest donors.“The problem is the outsized influence of industry. Take them on. Don't serve as an accomplice,” Katz wrote on X. “A total misread.”

news.title: Trump seeks to rebuild support among 2024 voters in North Carolina
news.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump will campaign in North Carolina on Wednesday ​for Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley, his first major campaign stop since the Republican Party's midterm convention as he begins ‌a nationwide effort to make the 2026 elections a referendum on his presidency.

The visit comes as Trump seeks to help Whatley, a longtime Republican operative who previously chaired the Republican National Committee, close a polling gap against former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper.

Trump remains a powerful force with the Republican base, but Whatley will also need to ​win over North Carolina's large bloc of swing and unaffiliated voters as Republicans confront rising concerns over affordability that have strained ​Trump's support among more moderate voters.

Trump told Republicans at the convention in Dallas last week to "pretend that I'm on the ⁠ballot," even though he is not seeking election. He has vowed to make multiple campaign stops in battleground states and districts ahead of the November 3 ​elections.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in the past week found Trump's approval rating at 35%, up from a record-low 33% in the previous poll. Democrats led ​Republicans 44% to 37% on the generic congressional ballot, the widest Democratic advantage in the Reuters/Ipsos series since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

Fuel prices have added to the affordability challenge. The national average for regular gasoline was $4.33 a gallon on Tuesday, while diesel reached a record $6.27, according to AAA.

The North Carolina ​Senate race is open after Republican Senator Thom Tillis decided not to seek reelection amid a squabble with Trump that doomed his chances within ​the party. Cooper led Whatley 49% to 38% among likely voters in a recent Elon University poll, while 54% of North Carolina voters in the survey disapproved ‌of Trump's ⁠job performance and 31% approved.

The White House signaled that Trump will use the North Carolina event to highlight his administration's record on crime, a recurring theme in Whatley's campaign.

Whatley has work to do consolidating voters who backed Trump in 2024. An August Elon University poll found that 72% of voters who said they backed Trump supported Whatley, while 10% backed Cooper and 14% were undecided. Cooper, by comparison, was capturing 93% of voters ​who said they voted for Kamala ​Harris.

"Trump wins by roughly three points ⁠in '24, largely because those independents decided that he was going to be better at handling the economy than Harris," said Jason Husser, director of the Elon University Poll and a political science professor. "But he's disappointed them. ​They're not saying the economy is going great, and oftentimes they're pointing to his policies as reasons for ​it."

Unaffiliated voters account ⁠for roughly 40% of North Carolina's registered electorate, making them the state's largest registration bloc.

"It's mathematically impossible to win the state without winning unaffiliated voters," said veteran Republican strategist Paul Shumaker, a former adviser to Tillis. "We Republicans have to understand that we have to address the affordability issue, and we have ⁠to be ​able to put unaffiliated voters' minds at ease as it relates to the economy ​and affordability between now and November for the Senate race to remain in play."

Democrats are seeking to make the race a referendum on Trump and his policies.

"Whatley has tied himself ​to Trump and, given the polls, I would not be doing that," said North Carolina Democratic Party Chairwoman Anderson Clayton.
news.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump will campaign in North Carolina on Wednesday ​for Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley, his first major campaign stop since the Republican Party's midterm convention as he begins ‌a nationwide effort to make the 2026 elections a referendum on his presidency.

news.title: Stephen Colbert’s nuclear reaction to CBS as Jimmy Kimmel brings him on late night show
news.text:
Stephen Colbert has returned to late night in a special guest appearance on Jimmy Kimmel’s show.

Colbert, 62, has not appeared in a late slot since the cancelation of his eponymous CBS show, which aired its final episode in May.

When Kimmel told the former host he looked “happier” and “healthier” at Monday’s Emmy Awards — during which Colbert won a trophy for the final season of his show — Colbert didn’t mince words about why.

“Like, I don’t drink a cup of poison every day?” Colbert began. “Because part of the job is… the old gig as I remember it was to be lowered like carbon rods into a radioactive pool every day and then to be pulled out and put in front of a camera and to irradiate it back at the audience at a non-lethal rad level.”

“That’s exactly the job description,” Kimmel joked.

Colbert added that he no longer stresses about the issues that are discussed on late night television, saying, “I have an opportunity to not think about the news every day, and I took it.” 

Kimmel went on to ask Colbert about his Emmys haul after the former host said The Late Show with Stephen Colbert won seven trophies for its final season.

“Did anyone from CBS call to congratulate you on your seven Emmys?” Kimmel asked.

“I am not familiar with that organization. Thank you for asking. Yes,” Colbert responded sarcastically.

CBS announced the cancelation of the late night show in July 2025, just days after Colbert criticized the network’s parent company, Paramount, for reaching a $16 million settlement with President Donald Trump over accusations that its newsmagazine series 60 Minutes deceptively edited a 2024 interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris. CBS staffers told The Independent it was a continuation of the “Trump shakedown” that began with the settlement.

Colbert’s latest jab at the network came hours after he commented about Bari Weiss, the former conservative political commentator with no previous broadcast experience who was made editor-in-chief of CBS News in October 2025, after Paramount merged with Skydance. 

After the Emmys, Colbert was asked about Weiss by CNN correspondent Elizabeth Wagmeister and Variety’s co-editor-in-chief Ramin Setoodeh, per The Daily Beast.

Colbert said he had “never heard of her” before adding sarcastically, “Do you know her? I hear great things.”

After receiving a standing ovation for winning the Emmy for Outstanding Variety Series, Colbert plugged his show’s writers, urging others in the industry to hire them.

“They will make your show better, and they will make your day easier,” he said.

“I want to say to the audience, thank you so much for watching,” Colbert continued. “We hope you enjoyed the show. We had a great time doing it for you.”
news.summary: Colbert’s late night appearance came after he won an Emmy for the final season of his eponymous show

news.title: Two-thirds of Americans see risk of AI destroying humanity: Poll
news.text: A majority of Americans think advanced artificial intelligence carries at least a moderate risk of eventually destroying humanity, according to a poll released Wednesday, highlighting growing public concern over the rapid development of AI technology.About two-thirds of respondents said there is at least "a moderate risk" that advanced AI could destroy humanity, including 17% who said it is "almost certain" and 20% who described the risk as "significant," according to a new poll released by Politico.Another 26% characterized the risk as moderate.The survey found concern across political, gender and age groups.Among voters in the 2024 presidential election, 70% of those who voted for Democratic candidate Kamala Harris saw at least a moderate risk, compared with 60% of Donald Trump voters.President Trump has downplayed the fears about AI.Americans also expressed greater support for slowing AI development than for continuing to build increasingly advanced systems.According to the poll, 48% said AI is "good enough," and development should be paused to reduce risks, while 31% favored continued development because advanced AI could bring significant benefits. Among Harris voters, 58% backed a pause, compared with 44% of Trump voters.The findings come as prominent AI industry figures have publicly warned about the technology's potential dangers. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, alongside billionaire Elon Musk, have called for slowing the development of advanced AI.About half of Americans surveyed said AI leaders warning that the technology could ultimately kill humanity genuinely believe their warnings. By contrast, 26% said such statements are intended as marketing to make AI products appear more powerful or important.Trump has continued to emphasize AI development as an economic and technological priority, while dismissing warnings about existential risks. Republicans and Democrats in Washington are nevertheless debating how to balance AI safeguards with the need for the U.S. to remain competitive with China.The poll was conducted online by London-based Public First on Sept. 13-15 among 2,064 U.S. adults. It has a margin of error of plus or minus 2.2 percentage points, with higher margins for smaller subgroups.

news.title: Women Built MAHA. MAGA Bros Have Taken It Over.
news.text:
Editor’s Note: When Robert F. Kennedy Jr. jumped on Donald Trump’s bandwagon in 2024, he brought with him the wellness-obsessed, vaccine-rejecting, food label-reading Make America Healthy Again voters who’ve been credited with helping Trump take back the White House. But there are signs that the MAHA–MAGA alliance is wearing thin, from squabbles over inaction to a tense standoff over regulating the herbicide glyphosate. In our MAHA and the Midterms series, a partnership between Mother Jones and the Food & Environment Reporting Network, we consider how MAHA is shaping the political landscape and upcoming elections.

This past February, as Super Bowl viewers chowed down on Buffalo wings and loaded nachos, they found themselves unexpectedly admonished. On their TV screens, in a black-and-white close-up, was former heavyweight champion and convicted rapist Mike Tyson, ripping his teeth through a carrot as though it were Evander Holyfield’s ear. “We’re the most powerful country in the world,” Tyson said. “And we have the most obese, fudgy people.” As he tore into an apple, white block script was superimposed over his face: “Processed Food Kills. Eat Real Food.” 

The ad directed viewers to RealFood.gov, a website laying out the new food pyramid, a pet project of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. that literally flipped the previous model on its head: Now, whole grains are at the pointy bottom and protein, dairy, and fats get top billing. The ad was sponsored by the nonprofit MAHA Center, whose leader, publisher Tony Lyons, also co-founded MAHA pac. And it signaled a telling shift. This wasn’t your mother’s Make America Healthy Again (or Gwyneth Paltrow’s, for that matter). This was manly MAHA.

Much attention has been paid to the MAHA moms, and rightly so. Women have powered the movement, evangelizing for whole foods and raw milk on Instagram, urging President Donald Trump to appoint Kennedy to lead HHS, and protesting against food additives and agricultural chemicals, in particular glyphosate, found in the weed killer Roundup.

But it’s the movement’s men who have ascended to the highest levels of power. RFK Jr. is the most prominent, but the list also includes Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services; Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, who is running the National Institutes of Health; and Dr. Marty Makary, who was commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration until he resigned earlier this year. And it’s not just in government. Health entrepreneur turned MAHA stalwart Calley Means is the man who suggested that Kennedy forge an alliance with Trump and remains an influential adviser to Kennedy at HHS. His sister, Casey, meanwhile, was a vaccine-skeptical doctor nominated for surgeon general—only to watch her prospects die in the Senate.

With the midterm elections approaching and MAHA voters increasingly dissatisfied with Trump, it’s worth asking: How exactly did a cause powered by women turn into one run by men? And will the women who built the MAHA movement ever revolt?

MAHA is often characterized by its most scientifically questionable positions—opposition to vaccines and fluoride, a fondness for raw milk and beef tallow—but the truth is that it is a complex coalition. Surveys conducted by Politico suggest that the movement’s core priorities are what you might hear from any athleisure-clad shopper circling the outer perimeter of Whole Foods: fewer ultraprocessed foods, food dyes, forever chemicals, microplastics, and pesticides, and more physical movement. 

Kennedy speaks all of these languages. His anti-vaccine activism gets the most press, but he has rallied against polluters and frequently inveighs against ultraprocessed Frankenfoods pushed on the public by corporations. In the lead-up to the 2024 election, food journalist Mark Bittman asked in The New York Times why Americans were hearing more about food from Trump than they were from Kamala Harris. The intersection of food, chemicals, chronic illness, and corporate power may not have been central for most voters. But it was a topic with significant social media reach, especially to the young, female, and politically disengaged—and that pulled many who might otherwise share a Democrat’s politics into Trump’s orbit. 

Kelly Ryerson, a prominent MAHA leader who writes under the name “Glyphosate Girl,” came to the movement the way many women do: because of personal health problems that traditional medicine couldn’t solve. Attending a gluten sensitivity conference, she heard it suggested that the issue might not be the gluten itself, but rather the chemicals sprayed on American wheat. That started her down a glyphosate research rabbit hole and eventually, in 2018, to the San Francisco courtroom where Monsanto, the manufacturer of glyphosate, was being sued by a man claiming the herbicide caused his cancer. One of the lawyers on the case was RFK Jr. 

“I’m politically independent,” Ryerson told me. “I feel that I really represent this massive group of women who have either their family member, their child, or they themselves have been struggling with some kind of chronic illness and are just fed up with the toxicity.” Ryerson, like other MAHA devotees, stuck with Kennedy even as he switched parties. 

That came in the summer of 2024, as Kennedy’s own presidential campaign was lagging. When Trump was shot at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, Calley Means reportedly called Kennedy and “suggested that it might be a moment for unity—Mr. Trump had just narrowly escaped the same fate that had befallen Mr. Kennedy’s father and uncle,” according to The New York Times. By the end of August, Kennedy was out of the race and in Trump’s camp, and MAHA was an emergent force in American politics. 

Ryerson, “Food Babe” Vani Hari, and other MAHA influencers supported the McDonald’s-eating Trump in large part because of his association with Kennedy. And, Ryerson says, while much of the MAHA movement’s true devotion was and is with Kennedy, its followers were smart enough to see that Trump’s idiosyncratic and unpredictable politics were a potential asset. “The thought behind Trump,” Ryerson said, “was that it was the only way forward with getting Kennedy into a role.” And she also believed that “the chemical industry has its grips so tightly on both parties that it’s like, well, we need someone that we might have a chance of him saying, ‘No, we’re done with that.’ And Trump is so volatile in many different ways, you don’t know which way he’s going to go.” Maybe, she thought, he would go hers. 

Spoiler alert: He hasn’t. Rather than forcing food and chemical companies to clean up their acts, the Trump administration’s senior health officials seem to be more preoccupied with the priorities of the manosphere. MAHA, says Monika McDermott, a professor of political science at Fordham University, “fits with the MAGA movement’s vision of the role that men play and the roles that women play. And so, yeah, women are figureheads and can do things about the family, but the experts are still the masculine figures.”

For expertise, they’ve turned to a smattering of “functional medicine” doctors (healthcare providers who focus on “root causes” of disease, like diet, exercise, and sleep), researchers, and activists, most of whom have podcasts or large social media followings, such as Dr. Mark Hyman and Calley Means. Before becoming an adviser to RFK Jr., Means co-founded a company called Truemed that helps consumers use tax-advantaged medical savings accounts, like HSAs and FSAs, to buy things like red-light therapy boxes, Meta glasses, and supplements. (Hyman is an investor in the company, which also sells his recommended supplements.)

The administration’s MAHA-adjacent decisions also have prioritized the interests of men. Take protein. Like anxieties about testosterone and “soy boys”—weak men supposedly feminized by eating too much tofu instead of red meat—the protein craze is as much about a robust male identity as it is nutrition.

“There’s been a steady drumroll of protein boosterism by characters in the manosphere who trade in ideas that masculinity is in decline and under attack,” says Samantha King, a professor in the School of Kinesiology and Health Studies at Queen’s University in Canada and co-author of Protein: The Making of a Nutritional Superstar. Joe Rogan, the megapopular podcaster whose endorsement of Trump was widely seen as boosting his support among young men, has complained that masculinity is unfairly vilified, while hawking protein supplements and talking about his own penchant for eating wild game. He went on a fully carnivore diet for a 30-day challenge, which resulted in “hellacious projectile doo-doo.” Popular manosphere figure Andrew Tate, who with his brother was fighting extradition to the United Kingdom for alleged rape and sex trafficking as of this writing, told Tucker Carlson in 2023 that “80 percent of my calories come from meat. I have 10 cups of coffee a day and three or four large cigars.” “Smoking is fantastic for your testosterone level,” he added. (The Tates have denied all charges filed against them.) 

No one seems more dedicated to protein than RFK Jr. When he announced the inverted food pyramid earlier this year, he framed it as a triumphal end to the war on protein—a dog whistle, King said, for the war on men, and especially on the male manual worker. RFK Jr. claims to subsist almost exclusively on meat and fermented foods, a diet that has, according to The Wall Street Journal, been embraced by Vice President JD Vance, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, to no doubt pungent results. And let’s not forget the weird video that RFK Jr. made with Kid Rock, in which they both exercised shirtless in a sauna (Kennedy in jeans), before pounding milk in a hot tub. 

Meanwhile, in the first year of Kennedy’s tenure, HHS announced the appointment of “five new agency leaders to advance MAHA goals.” Four of the five were men. The most prominent was Admiral Brian Christine, an “internationally recognized leader in men’s health” and the new assistant secretary for health at HHS. 

As part of his mandate, Christine, a staunch anti-abortion Catholic, was responsible for overseeing the agency administering Title X, the federal family planning program that has traditionally funded contraception access for poor women across America. Earlier this year, HHS released radically revamped guidance for organizations applying for Title X grants. “Chronic disease” gets 14 mentions in the document; contraception gets one. Relatively little attention is given to helping women prevent unwanted pregnancy, the reason the Title X program was created in the first place. Much more is spent on male fertility concerns: testosterone levels, sperm counts and motility, avoiding pornography, and so on. In recent months, testosterone therapy has also become a new general HHS priority. In early September, The Washington Sun reported that the department had canceled more than half of the Office of Minority Health’s existing grants, focused on things like infant mortality and postpartum wellness, to instead prioritize programs devoted to exercise and the “root causes” of infertility, including erectile disfunction.

At the same time, the administration has been mostly unwilling to regulate Big Food and Big Ag—the MAHA moms’ main priority. After Trump appointed industry-friendly Lee Zeldin to run the Environmental Protection Agency, Zeldin immediately went on a deregulation spree, staffed the agency with former Big Ag and industry lobbyists, and appointed former industry representatives to oversee pesticide regulation. The EPA office once charged with research on toxic chemicals has been dismantled. 

And then there is the administration’s actions related to glyphosate, long one of MAHA’s top targets. Earlier this year, Trump issued an executive order calling glyphosate critical for national security and urging production increases. In June, the Supreme Court sided with chemical giant Bayer, which acquired Monsanto in 2018, in a case related to its weed killer Roundup. Trump’s DOJ had advocated for the court to take on the case. On Forked, a food politics podcast, Ryerson called the administration’s role in the case “deeply, deeply devastating.”

So where does all this leave the MAHA moms? Ryerson says that while MAHA men are largely the ones in the most powerful roles in government, women “are still dictating it from the grassroots,” and “if what we want isn’t happening, then they won’t win reelection.” 

She, podcaster Alex Clark, and others have been warning Republicans that if they don’t show up for the women of MAHA, the women of MAHA may stop showing up for them. At the Turning Point USA Women’s Leadership Summit over the summer, Clark told a conservative interviewer, “I believe that we won 2024 because of these women; I believe if these women are ignored, we’re going to lose the midterms, and I believe we will lose 2028.” 

Ryerson, for her part, said she’s still stunned that most Democrats in Congress haven’t jumped on these issues. One exception is Maine Rep. Chellie Pingree, who told The 19th: “I really don’t think that these are necessarily left or right. The questions around toxins in our food and food is medicine, and the opposition to Big Ag and big chemical companies is very universal.” 

This dynamic—of women as foot soldiers while men take up command posts—is not unique to MAHA. The “wine moms” who powered Democratic victories in the suburbs for the last several election cycles, and the Black women who took on the lion’s share of the legwork of “souls to the polls” turnout machines, did most of the labor—and were often mocked instead of being credited. But they eventually translated that preparation into power: 43 percent of congressional Democrats are now female (for Republicans, it’s 15 percent); women account for nearly half of state Democratic legislators. Will MAHA’s largely female organizers and leaders take a similar path within the GOP—or will the Democratic Party convince them to defect? 

Ryerson says that she continues to support Kennedy and that anecdotally, many MAHA women in her orbit believe he’s often hamstrung by the White House but still a force for good. And many Democrats are understandably hesitant to court followers of a movement they see as rife with dangerous quackery. But most of MAHA’s core issues—additives in food, microplastics, pesticides—used to be clearly Democratic issues. If Democrats were to back away from them now, Ryerson says, they’re leaving votes on the table. 

MAHA voters, she says, are “up for grabs, and [politicians] should be battling it out to see who can propose the best exit out of this toxic world that we’re living in.”

This story was produced with the Food & Environment Reporting Network.

news.title: Anthony Scaramucci: Farage is a dumber version of Trump
news.text:
Anthony Scaramucci is a man of many stripes. Former Donald Trump adviser, one-time White House official, financier, broadcaster and, it turns out, astrologer.

We are sitting at the table of a swanky west London hotel to discuss his upcoming book – a tell-all memoir covering US politics from his front-row seat, which featured an infamous 11-day stint as Trump’s White House communications director – but the first thing Scaramucci wants to talk about is star signs.

Within a few minutes, he has used my age and birthday to analyse my romantic relationship and diagnose my personality traits with surprising accuracy. I ask about Trump’s horoscope. “He’s a classic Gemini,” he replies in a broad New York accent, referring to the sign typically symbolised by a good and bad twin. In the President’s case though, both are “evil”.

There is perhaps some celestial irony that Scaramucci’s own birthday is 6 January, the date now immortalised by the Capitol attack of 2021, when about 2,000 Trump supporters smashed through the seat of the US Congress, demanding the result of the presidential election be overturned. It was the zenith of a political movement that Scaramucci helped to build – and now sees as his mission to tear down.

A long-term Republican donor and founder of investment firm SkyBridge Capital, Scaramucci worked as an adviser on Trump’s presidential transition team and was a top official at the Export-Import Bank – the US Government’s export credit agency – before joining the White House as communications director in July 2017.

The appointment of Scaramucci, an acquaintance of real estate mogul Trump from the New York social scene, led to the resignation of White House chief of staff Reince Priebus and spokesman Sean Spicer.

Ten days into his tenure, he was sacked after making disparaging comments about administration officials in a conversation he thought was off the record.

Now, at 62, “The Mooch” has become a broadcasting star – he hosts podcast The Rest Is Politics: US alongside BBC correspondent Katty Kay – and one of the US President’s harshest critics. He describes his support for Trump as the “biggest mistake of his life”.

“It’s as if a bully got the top job,” Scaramucci says of Trump’s election. “You want a benevolent uncle who’s sitting on the most powerful military and the most powerful economy in the world to help oversee the world, but you got a bully.”

The presidency was, he believes, a lifelong goal of Trump’s – not, as was rumoured, a response to teasing from Barack Obama at the 2011 White House Correspondents’ Dinner. Trump has a “massive chip on his shoulder”, Scaramucci says, though he still hasn’t figured out exactly why. “I’m not a psychotherapist, but it’s very important for him to force himself into the world, right? He’s got to have his name plastered on every building. He’s got to have different brands associated with his name.”

But he is nothing if not tenacious, adds Scaramucci, noting Trump’s capacity for bouncing back – from bankrupt businesses to reality TV and later, the presidency. “On a scale of one to 10, what is his resilience? It’s a 10. Coming back from failure? It’s a 10. You can hate the guy, but I’m just telling you,” he says. “He’s an incredibly hard worker. You can’t look at a guy who’s 80 and say he doesn’t have energy and he doesn’t have a robust personality.”

Trump’s stellar recovery is not unlike that of the indefatigable Scaramucci himself, who turned his ill-fated stint in the White House into a successful media career and is now worth an estimated $200m (£148m), thanks to his hedge fund and hosting popular crypto conferences. He will appear in Sky’s four-part “constructed documentary” series The Wargame from next week, alongside former UK cabinet ministers Michael Gove and Penny Mordaunt as well as former Scottish first minister Nicola Sturgeon.

Yet in their outlook, the two men are poles apart. Scaramucci recalls a TV appearance where he was asked about the US President’s comments on four Democratic congresswomen known as The Squad – all women of colour – in which Trump said they should go back to the countries they came from. Three of them are American-born and the other is a naturalised US citizen who came to America as a child.

“I said, that’s a nativist, racist thing to say,” he says. “They said that to my Italian American grandmother in the 1920s. It hurt her feelings. She used to always talk about that with us. None of us speaks Italian because of that; because my grandmother was afraid of that racism.”

Trump is often accused of having no ideology, taking a purely transactional approach to decisions honed in his real-estate past. Scaramucci doesn’t agree. Instead, he categorises the 80-year-old’s ideology as one of three components: isolationism, xenophobia and anti-immigration.

Scaramucci believes that Trump and Steve Bannon (his former White House adviser, ex-convict and prominent Maga broadcaster) have a vision of an America that has been taken for granted by the world and should be walled off – at times, literally. “They would rather have the plastic cup made in the US for $5 (£3.70) than in China for five cents,” he says.

Despite some failures – he cites Afghanistan and Iraq – Scaramucci believes that the US has helped raise living standards around the world and, through legal migration, its own “intellectual capital” at home.

He recognises some of the Trumpian politics here in Britain, describing Reform UK leader Nigel Farage as a “dumber version of Trump”.

“He has Trump’s guile and shamelessness, and he’s got Trump’s corruptibility. But Trump is smart. He got to the American presidency twice. Farage doesn’t have the political instincts Trump has; he doesn’t have the bombast and the flair. In 2016, Trump had almost 100 per cent name recognition. Farage doesn’t have that.”

Farage has long aligned himself with Trump, making regular trips to the US, calling him a friend and suggesting his presidency bodes well for Reform.

Police are investigating Reform UK over allegations it broke foreign funding laws, which the party denies. Farage has personally come under parliamentary scrutiny for not declaring a £5m donation from a crypto billionaire. He said he did not need to do so because he received it before he became MP for Clacton and it was not political.

Two of Farage’s close advisers, Dan Jukes and James Orr, resigned this summer after a Channel 4 investigation appeared to show them discussing ways to get around electoral law. 

Critics of the US President say he has been equally destructive abroad as at home, launching a war in Iran which has killed thousands, spooking the global economy, turning on allies and ditching international institutions. “If you said to me that in my lifetime an American president would reject Nato, threaten the invasion of Greenland, post pictures of putting the American flag over the provinces of Canada and Mexico and Greenland, I would tell you: that’s absolutely mad,” Scaramucci says.

He is particularly incredulous at Trump’s decision to cut back military aid to Ukraine as it faces a brutal Russian invasion, particularly after the 1994 treaty with Kyiv, when it handed over nuclear weapons in exchange for security guarantees.

“Putin has a hold on Donald Trump, and I don’t know why,” Scaramucci says, echoing fears around the US President’s threats to Nato and repetition of Russian rhetoric that – inadvertently or not – appears to play into the Russian leader’s hands. “We have an agent for Vladimir Putin at the top of the American government.”

A US government report found systematic Russian attempts to interfere with the 2016 election, including a social media campaign in support of Trump and intelligence work against Hillary Clinton. The New York Times exposed phone records and intercepted calls that showed Trump associates had repeated contacts with senior Russian intelligence officials in the year before the election. Trump admitted that his son met a Russian lawyer to garner information on his opponent but argued it was legal.

“Trump challenging our electoral integrity in our country is full-on cynicism that somebody like Vladimir Putin would want in the West,” Scaramucci says.

On Venezuela, however, he thinks Trump was right. “Even though I despise the guy, he does deserve that win,” he says, noting that Nicolás Maduro was an unelected dictator and his removal was “a net positive to the West”.

Trump’s latest target is Ireland, with his comments supporting Irish reunification during his weekend visit threatening to blow open tensions there. But Scaramucci brushes this off. “I think if it was said by Barack Obama or Bill Clinton or a president that was viewed as a normal person and not a bipolar maniac, I think it would be taken more seriously. But I think that commentary will be wrapping fish in two weeks.”

Scaramucci may have done a U-turn on Trump, but believes the US President too has changed, morphing into a “hard-right ultra-nationalist and an ardent and strident social conservative”. His slide to the right has been accompanied by growing concerns about his health. Earlier this year, 30 senior doctors signed a statement declaring Trump was mentally unfit to serve and that his ability to launch nuclear weapons was a “danger” to the world.

Scaramucci has previously claimed Trump has been “losing it, mentally” but dismisses theories that the President has dementia as “BS”, putting the change down to a combination of age and status. Trump became the oldest US president to be sworn in to office when he returned to power in February 2025 aged 78.

“Has he declined? We’re all declining,” says Scaramucci. “There’s also the imperial nature of the presidency: the majesty, the power, the pomp, which has also changed him. Obama said it better than me: the presidency, if you’re a good guy coming into the presidency, you can magnify your good-guyness. If you’re a bad guy coming into the presidency, guess what? It’s going to magnify your bad-guyness.”

With such ideological chasms between Scaramucci and his former boss, how did he end up as Trump’s professional attack dog?

“I’m a 30-year Republican presidential fundraiser,” he explains. His political work began with Bob Dole in 1996, and in the 2016 Republican primaries, he worked for candidates Scott Walker and Jeb Bush before they dropped out of the race. Trump was his third choice, Scaramucci says, and he initially didn’t take the tycoon’s candidacy seriously.

“Like most Republicans, I was reluctant to be with him, and I ended up with him by default because he won. Now, I have said it repeatedly, and I’ll say it to you, that was probably the biggest mistake of my career. Jeb Bush told me not to go work for him. I didn’t listen to him.”

Over time, Scaramucci says he got “sucked in like everybody else”.

He adds: “You get sucked into your own bullshit of power and significance, and then you start to equivocate, and then you start to lose yourself. You become a moral hypocrite like everybody else that goes to work for Donald Trump.”

It was a mistake that nearly cost him his marriage. In July 2017, Scaramucci’s pregnant wife Deidre Ball filed for divorce, and later that month he missed the birth of his son James because he was on board Air Force One. The couple later reconciled.

Many Republicans, Scaramucci argues, are “still lying to themselves, trying to justify their support of Trump and all the stupid shit that they do”.

He insists: “I don’t do that. I say: the guy’s a f**king asshole.”

But he believes the tide is turning on Trump. Republicans on the campaign trail are, he says, distancing themselves from the President, scrubbing his name from websites and campaign posters. His approval rating is hovering around 33 per cent of registered voters, a record low.

Trump supporters, Scaramucci thinks, are experiencing “buyer’s remorse”. A quarter of his fans are diehard and will be with him no matter what because of the “anger-based politics” that exists now, he believes, but independents feel misled. Trump promised to lower prices and end forever wars, but has increased both, he adds.

Polling indicates that the Republicans will be punished for this at November’s midterm elections, losing the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate. But if the Democrats pick a leader further to the left, they could still lose, Scaramucci believes, saying Americans “don’t like wokeism and the culture war stuff”. At the next presidential election, his money would be on California Governor Gavin Newsom or Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, both of whom he believes could beat almost any Republican.

Despite Trump’s comments on 2028, Scaramucci disputes theories that the President will try to change the constitution to give himself another term in office. He thinks the US government will be able to constrain Trump, or that the President will struggle to pull it off. “The good news about Trump is he’s very disorganised. He has the attention span of a fruit fly. He’s going to be 82, and he’s universally disliked. If he was 51, I’d say: you’ve got a huge problem with this guy.”

In response to Scaramucci’s criticism, White House spokesman Davis Ingle told The i Paper: “Anthony Scaramucci lasted 11 short days in the White House. He makes lightweights look credible.”

When Trump eventually departs the Oval Office, Scaramucci is not sure how long it will take the Republicans to return to the “old legacy party” he supported. But he believes the “populist anger” gripping America, fuelled by spiralling inflation, won’t disappear overnight: “This is economic desperation, as opposed to aspiration.”

His new book, he says, is an attempt to unpick how the US got here. It is not a hit piece, nor is it tribal, he insists. There are well-intentioned characters of different political persuasions – like Barack Obama and George Bush, who Scaramucci feels were trying to do the right thing – as well as villains. Trump falls in the latter category, with Scaramucci describing him as a fundamentally “malevolent person”.

He says: “It’s an objective observation of mistakes that we made, Democrats and Republicans… that led to the anger-based populism that we’re living in today. I believe that the platform I’ve been given, due to the infamy of my firing, is giving me a standing to at least object to what is going on and to offer some ideas.”

Would he ever run for office himself? “I’m not well suited for that.” Why? “I don’t think I’m a congenital liar,” he says, smiling. He would, however, be willing to back another candidate with fundraising and media support.

Though his fall from power may have been dramatic, it is clear Scaramucci is far from done with US politics. After his role in creating the problem, he says: “I would like to be part of the solution.”

All the Wrong Moves by Anthony Scaramucci (The Bodley Head, £25) is published on 17 September

Key context

Anthony Scaramucci studied at Harvard Law School before beginning his Wall Street career at Goldman Sachs and going on to become an influential figure in the cryptocurrency and blockchain world. He has written six books

He was fired from the Trump administration after giving a profanity-laced interview to The New Yorker in which he called White House chief of staff Reince Priebus a “paranoid schizophrenic” and made vulgar comments about chief strategist Steve Bannon

Scaramucci is a long-term Republican donor but his support has shifted across party lines. He fundraised for Barack Obama’s 2008 presidential campaign (later asking Obama when he would “stop whacking Wall Street like a piñata“) and donated to Hillary Clinton before serving as national finance co-chair for Republican Mitt Romney’s 2012 presidential campaign and becoming a Trump backer. In the 2024 presidential elections, he supported Kamala Harris

news.title: Voters skeptical Trump will ever deliver his promised $5,000 dividend checks, new poll shows
news.text:
President Donald Trump’s promise to send out a $5,000 check to every American adult if Republicans hang on to the House of Representatives and Senate in November’s midterms is being met with deep skepticism, a new poll has found. 

The president made the pledge in his headline address at last week’s Republican National Convention in Dallas, Texas, branding it the “Trump Dividend” and telling his supporters: “If the Republicans win, you win with us.”

However, it was quickly pointed out that such a policy would cost the Treasury at least $1.3 trillion and invited accusations of bribery and questions over its legality. 

Now, a new Economist/YouGov poll has found that 61 percent of likely midterms voters say they think Trump will definitely not or probably not deliver on the checks, with just 22 percent saying they believe he will and the remainder unsure either way. 

The same survey found that opinion on the checks themselves was evenly divided, with 45 percent of likely voters opposed to the idea but 43 percent in favor of it.

The demographics most excited about the checks were MAGA Republicans and people aged 18 to 29, who were 69 percent and 61 percent in favor respectively.

Conversely, the groups most opposed included Democrats and over 65s (only 39 percent were in favor in each case), college graduates and liberals (37 percent) and people who voted for Kamala Harris in 2024 (30 percent).

Possible reasons for the skepticism include Trump’s failure to provide any detailed information about where the money will actually come from and the fact that the president has a track record of promising the public cash without delivering.

He did send out stimulus checks bearing his signature during the Covid-19 pandemic but more recently claimed that money saved by DOGE cuts to the federal bureaucracy and raked in by his since-blocked reciprocal tariffs policy would be paid out to voters. 

Those promises would have been worth a combined $7,000 per person but neither ever came to pass.

Trump did pay out $1,776 “Warrior Dividend” checks to serving members of the military last Christmas, however, and invoked that gesture in his convention speech as proof he could deliver. 

When The Independent asked the White House last week where the president hoped to source the money for his checks from, spokesperson Davis Ingle hit out at the “doomers and naysayers” he said had consistently underestimated Trump but did not provide any more concrete answers about the source of funding.

Vice President JD Vance told Fox News the day after Trump’s announcement that it could come from tariff revenue. 

“We’re taking in an extraordinary amount of revenue because the president of the United States is actually standing up to both foreign companies, but also foreign countries who’ve been taking advantage of America’s workers for pretty much my entire life,” he said.

However, the estimated $132.5 billion drawn in from net customs revenue since January 2025 would not come close to the $1.3 trillion needed to make the payout.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has meanwhile told NBC News the administration will “earn the money that Donald Trump wants to pay out, not from the deficit and not from taxpayers,” likewise failing to offer specifics. 

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also declined to give a definitive answer when pressed by the House Financial Services Committee Tuesday.

Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson has said the policy would require congressional approval, which the president could not hope to secure without control of both chambers, hence the victory condition he placed on the promise.
news.summary: Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they doubt President Trump will deliver on his midterms ‘dividend’ pledge, with just 22 percent thinking he will follow through, survey finds

news.title: The very real scenario where the GOP expands its Senate majority
news.text:
The New York Times ran a splashy story this week with its experts predicting the outcome of the midterm elections. Overall, “It’s looking bullish for Democrats,” said the alleged paper of record, with not one of these experts giving the GOP an outright majority in the upper chamber.

It’s increasingly difficult to trust pollsters these days given their track record. Nate Silver, for example, is one of these five experts the New York Times offers up in the piece. He’s the same guy who gave Hillary Clinton about a 75% chance of winning the 2016 presidential race. He also predicted Kamala Harris would top Donald Trump both in the popular vote and Electoral College in 2024.
